#10093. AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.

AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.

Research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which was, unbeknownst to users, copying secrets to a hidden file and committing them with the rest of the developer's code.

Among specific secrets leaked were "a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database," Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote in the post.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, "from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors," they wrote.

The issue stems from how coding assistants — Claude Code, in a specific case that the researchers examined — carry out certain commands. "Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file," the researchers explained.

The tool will ask the user before running the command and, if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," then "it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder," according to the report.

"Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code," the researchers explained.

The fact that a routine development task creates a security exposure is dangerous for organizations, especially because these AI coding tools are supposed to be helpful, not harmful, notes Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing for database security firm Liquibase.

“A developer approves a command to save time, the AI agent retains credentials as part of that approval, and those credentials can eventually end up in a public repository," he observes via email. "Nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible."

In the case of Claude Code, Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, finding that 1,122 files contained real secrets. The researchers identified 1,379 distinct secrets in those files alone, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

Claude Code is not being overtly careless; it does try to protect files when it creates its .claude/settings.local.json file inside a Git repository, the researchers noted. The tool does this by adding the file to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore the file on that particular developer's machine. This prevents it from being included in routine commits.

However, the protection is not built into the development project itself, and the "ignore" rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, the researchers noted. "The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it," they wrote.

Moreover, Claude Code itself was sometimes responsible for committing the exposed files. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file.

The action that exposes these secrets while using Claude Code appears to be a "dead zone" of sorts for developers using AI coding assistants, so they likely have no idea that they've just exposed a secret, observes Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock.

Related:Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

"A 'don't ask again' prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file, and many developers clicking it likely don't know that file exists," he says. "Once it lands in a repository, it sits in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through."

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing the findings. After their publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, said in public comments that although Claude Code historically has not done secrets scrubbing, the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure described by Apiiro, according to Apiiro's report.

Those approaches may be to make sure auto mode catches the exposure, or to build in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas that Anthropic will prototype "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping something with its next version of Claude Code, Cherny said.

Indeed, the leakage exposes how Claude Code's protection relies heavily on a developer-specific Git setting rather than a safeguard built into the project or the AI coding tool itself, exposing a gap that can turn an ordinary command approval into a persistent credential leak.

To avoid this, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held, and open all fields and delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Meanwhile, security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repos, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

"As AI agents become more involved in software development, organizations need to recognize that source code isn't the only thing they need to secure," McCurdy observes. "Agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information, and traditional security checks may not catch everything."

She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. #10091. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#10090. How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Cloud Range's free 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment helps organizations identify gaps in operational technology (OT) incident response.

Cloud Range introduces a 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment to help organizations identify gaps in preparedness for cyberattacks affecting operational technology.

The assessment covers seven critical areas, from OT asset visibility and IT/OT coordination to incident detection, response, recovery, and readiness validation.

Recent OT cybersecurity research reinforces the importance of preparing IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to investigate and respond to attacks that can disrupt physical operations.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Cyberattacks affecting operational technology (OT) can disrupt production, equipment, and essential services, resulting in consequences that extend beyond disruptions to traditional IT systems. To help organizations evaluate their preparedness, Cloud Range today introduced the Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment, a free, 28-question resource designed to identify potential gaps in OT incident response preparedness.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

The assessment provides a practical starting point for IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to evaluate how well they understand their environments, coordinate responsibilities, and prepare to detect, investigate, respond to, and recover from cyber incidents affecting industrial operations.

“Organizations can have incident response plans, security tools, and experienced teams in place without knowing how effectively those capabilities will work together when an attack affects operations,” said Debbie Gordon, CEO of Cloud Range. “The first step is understanding where teams are prepared, where they may be relying on assumptions, and where further validation is needed. The stakes are different in OT because decisions made during a cyber incident can have direct operational consequences.”

Recent research illustrates the scale of cyber threats facing industrial organizations. The Dragos 2026 OT Cybersecurity Year in Review reports that approximately 3,300 industrial organizations were affected by ransomware in 2025.

Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 State of Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Report found that 59% of surveyed critical infrastructure organizations experienced a significant security breach in the past year. The research also found that 74% had not fully integrated IT and OT security operations, highlighting the importance of coordinated incident response.

The report also identifies operational consequences of cybersecurity incidents, including safety concerns, unplanned downtime, production disruptions, and financial losses.

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Together, these findings underscore a central challenge for organizations operating OT and industrial control systems (ICS): preventing attacks is important, but so is understanding whether teams can recognize, investigate, and respond quickly and effectively when incidents occur.

An attack does not have to originate within an OT network to affect industrial operations. Compromises involving enterprise IT systems, third-party access, supply chains, or interconnected infrastructure can create consequences for production environments and critical services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment examines seven areas that influence an organization's ability to prepare for and respond to cyberattacks affecting OT environments:

Know Your Environment: Understand critical OT assets, systems, dependencies, and connections between IT and OT environments.

Know Your Threats and Stakes: Recognize relevant cyber threats and their potential impact on operations, equipment, and safety.

Bridge IT and OT: Establish shared responsibilities, communication, and decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Detect and Investigate: Identify suspicious activity, investigate threats, and determine their potential operational consequences.

Respond Without Making It Worse: Make coordinated incident response decisions that account for production continuity, equipment, and safety.

Recover and Maintain Resilience: Understand recovery priorities, system dependencies, and procedures for restoring critical operations.

Prove Readiness Before It Matters: Validate response capabilities through realistic cyberattack simulations and measurable performance.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Each area includes three questions, with responses of Ready, Developing, or Unsure.

Rather than assigning a numerical score, the assessment helps organizations identify gaps, uncertainties, and areas requiring further attention. IT, security, OT, and engineering teams can complete it independently and compare their responses to uncover differences in understanding, unclear responsibilities, or differing assumptions about preparedness.

Why OT Incident Response Preparedness Requires Cross-Functional Coordination

OT environments present distinct incident response challenges because cyber decisions can affect physical equipment, industrial processes, production availability, and potentially safety.

Actions that may be appropriate in an enterprise IT environment, such as isolating a system or shutting down a device, can require additional operational evaluation when industrial systems are involved.

Effective OT incident response therefore depends on coordination among teams with different responsibilities and expertise.

IT and security personnel may focus on identifying malicious activity, containing threats, and investigating compromised systems. OT and engineering personnel understand process dependencies, equipment limitations, and the operational consequences of response decisions.

Both perspectives are essential. The integration gap identified in the Palo Alto Networks research reinforces the importance of shared understanding, clear responsibilities, and coordinated decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Understanding how to assess OT cyber readiness across these functions helps organizations identify where their procedures, communication, and decision-making may require further attention.

The assessment is intended to support those conversations before an actual incident demands coordinated action.

An assessment can help organizations identify preparedness gaps, but it cannot establish how effectively teams will perform during a real cyber incident.

That requires opportunities to investigate attacks, make decisions, coordinate across functions, and evaluate the results in realistic environments.

Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen critical infrastructure cyber readiness, realistic cloud-based OT/ICS, IT, cloud, and hybrid environments where teams can investigate cyber threats, coordinate incident response, and measure performance. Its critical infrastructure cybersecurity and readiness programs help organizations prepare for attacks that may disrupt industrial processes, equipment, and essential services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Range supports flat and Purdue-model industrial network architectures, allowing teams to investigate how connectivity, segmentation, and system dependencies influence attack progression and response. Hardware-in-the-loop capabilities can also connect physical OT laboratory equipment to the cyber range for cyber-physical security validation.

Through OT cyberattack simulations and adversary emulation, teams can investigate ransomware, supply-chain compromise, credential theft, lateral movement, and threats affecting industrial systems.

Performance metrics highlight how teams improve in detecting threats, investigating activity, coordinating decisions, and improving incident response over time.

Across Cloud Range customer engagements, measured improvements have included reductions of up to 66% in mean time to detect and improvements of up to 30% in overall incident response time. These results reflect broader cyber readiness programs and are not specific to OT environments.

As IT and OT environments become more interconnected, organizations face growing pressure to understand both their cybersecurity exposure and their ability to respond to incidents with operational consequences.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment provides a structured way to evaluate preparedness across seven critical areas. Organizations can use the findings to prioritize improvements and identify where realistic attack-based validation can provide stronger evidence of readiness.

The objective is not simply to have an incident response plan. It is to build confidence that the people, processes, and technologies involved can work together when an attack affects operations.

Cloud Range is the leader in Cyber Readiness and Validation, helping organizations continuously measure and improve how people, processes, and AI perform under real-world attack conditions. As the creator of the industry's first full-service, cloud-based cyber range, Cloud Range provides realistic IT, OT/ICS, and cloud environments where organizations can safely train, test, validate, measure, and benchmark cyber readiness across people, processes, and AI agents.

Used by enterprise organizations, government agencies, higher education institutions, critical infrastructure organizations, and managed security service providers (MSSPs), Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen cyber readiness through live-fire cyberattack simulations, objective performance measurement, expert guidance, continuous readiness programs, and AI validation.

Cloud Range has received multiple industry awards recognizing innovation and leadership in cyber readiness, cyber defense, and cybersecurity excellence and has been recognized by leading analyst and research organizations for its contributions to cyber readiness, cyber ranges, AI validation, and modern security operations. Learn more at cloudrangecyber.com.

#10089. Jujutsu Primer

This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.

jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git.

Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:

You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:

In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:

A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

The IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k.

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2.

Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested.

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:

On commit 849165bc, you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy, or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:

jj show shows commit details and a diff, which is empty here. $ jj show Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) Committer: Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) (no description set)

jj status shows repo state with diff stats. $ jj status The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : kpqxywon 849165bc (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config

jj diff works much like git diff. Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.

This output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show, we see this:

You’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty). The new commit ID for @ is 66b59f20, since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon. jj has no staging area like in git, so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

Let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run jj desc, which opens an editor, or provide it directly with -m.

Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable.

Now, let’s say we’re ready to use this new feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with jj new:

We’ve created an empty change nlrtlrxv on top of kpqxywon. jj status reflects that we are editing this new revision which does not yet differ from its parent.

jj commit is a shorthand for this common jj desc and jj new combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it.

To inspect the commit we just created (n), we can no longer use the bare jj show, which defaults to showing @. We have to pass the revision we want to inspect:

We can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a new commit on top of k to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature.

A separate jj desc would also work just fine instead of the -m flag on jj new. Here’s the current commit graph:

Note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between jj’s branchless model and git’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj new k, the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon. The jj log command has an -r flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q:

I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

Let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in qwyusntz we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change kpqxywon. We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to kpqxywon with jj edit:

Our working copy once again shows the changes from kpqxywon.

jj hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to q:

Instead of switching commits with jj edit k, we could have run jj edit @-. The revset @- is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands jj next [--edit] and jj prev [--edit] provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits.

If we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next jj invocation. For example, if we edit my_new_feature’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log, we’ll see that changes k, n, and q all get new commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase.

If the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex.

To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit…

In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any jj command, we’ll see that jj has marked the commit as unconflicted:

Let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In git, undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In jj, we can always run jj undo:

More generally, jj maintains a history of all actions in jj op log. We can inspect this log and jj op restore to a point in that history, or jj op revert an individual operation. If the jj undo itself was a mistake, we can jj redo.

The Hint in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow.

Editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your new changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

Let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a new commit on top of the conflicted commit:

Now we can resolve the conflicts in main.py in our editor, and rerun jj log:

We can inspect the diff in @ if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit:

The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work.

One of the powerful qualities of jj is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by jj undo, we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease.

Let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point.

Let’s use jj rebase to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit (q) should go between the implementation (k) and the usage (n). We could accomplish this by moving nlrtlrxv (and its empty descendant) on top of qwyusntz:

Another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n. Many jj commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. jj rebase --help documents these well.

Since arguments to jj rebase flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph.

If we wanted to insert a commit below k, the most direct way is jj new --before k, but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of r and rebase k:: on top:

If you enjoy using TUIs, jj arrange provides a commit graph editor similar to git rebase -i for reordering commits.

If we decided documentation should be in the same commit as implementation, we can squash:

jj will open an editor and give us a chance to write a combined commit message.

To drop a commit from the graph, we can use jj abandon. Let’s drop the preparation commit:

To abandon parts of a commit (hunks or changes to whole files), we can use the jj diffedit TUI (see docs).

The jj split TUI allows us to take a commit and split it into two consecutive commits by selecting which files or hunks should go in the first. Let’s use it to split up implementation and documentation again with jj split -r k:

The jj-hunk project provides a means to automate commit splitting. If you are so inclined, agents are quite good at using this tool to split up commits into a sequence of smaller changes for easier review.

jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub.

Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list.

Since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:

Now jj log shows our change with a correspondingly named bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk associated:

We’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the git_push_bookmark template config documented here. It’s a common pattern to format branch names like /.

Since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

To update a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward.

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

First, create a new commit on top of our branch. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: stzvpxow f14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files

Then make our edits. $ jj status Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : stzvpxow 6bdd43dc (no description set) Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature

Squash them into the bookmark branch. $ jj squash --from @ --into push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: xryuuprx 04d65a03 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature

We now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. $ jj git push -b push-nlrtlrxvuusk Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b]

The remote branch now reflects the new changes. The above output says that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

In this flow, we add new commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

Let’s first prepare the new commit. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: pptrztmx 6e49ff1f (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature

The bookmark does not automatically move to our new commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below:

There are several ways to move the bookmark to the new commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance, which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch, importing remote bookmarks:

And create a new empty commit on top of the remote branch:

Our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git, we see that from git’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.

This is because jj is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to git’s “current branch” state.

Syncing with the trunk (e.g. main) is just a specific example of this flow. We would jj git fetch to update our main to the upstream main, and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase my-branch on top of a new main:

jj commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this.

jjui is a TUI for jj that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it.

I prefer to have an always-live jj log in the corner of my screen by way of viddy (a nicer version of watch that supports color):

I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point:

You might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp, which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live jj log on the side and a terminal for running jj operations.

One of the biggest productivity gains from jj comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short.

Large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process.

Let’s say we’re building a new feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages:

jj’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR:

After you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls.

It’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with jj and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. jj-pancake is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon.

#10088. PostgreSQL 19 released

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has announced the release of PostgreSQL 19. Notable features in this release include the introduction of the REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) command to optimize tables without disruption to ongoing operations, better control over plan stability and query performance with the new pg_plan_advice extension, and a number of performance improvements.

In September, LWN covered the removal of several features initially slated for this release. See the release notes for a full list of new features and changes.

InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read

Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The update spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.

On the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.

Minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a new [ShortCircuit] attribute.

Developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that update a breaking change.

With 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.

SignalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.

Blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the new CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.

Developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.

For Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.

The release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.

On the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.

Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.

Two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the new UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.

Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.

For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's new in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

#10085. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#10084. F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

New AI Harms Taxonomy traces how harm moves through AI systems, from misleading chatbot answers to compromised autonomous agents, and identifies where defenses can intervene.

LOS ANGELES (November 10, 2026) — AI now shapes how we search, communicate, decide and run our digital lives. But when it goes wrong, how does it actually hurt people? F-Secure’s new AI Harms Taxonomy maps 26 distinct harms to consumers, tracing the path each one takes to reach a person. The result is a clear view of where protections can step in, and who is in the best position to help.

Developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, the taxonomy tackles a blind spot in how AI risk is discussed. Most frameworks list what could potentially go wrong, but stop short of connecting those harms to the systems and companies that could prevent them. F-Secure’s research goes further by mapping every layer between an AI-enabled threat and its impact on a consumer, then pinpointing where defenses need to go.

“As AI systems become more capable, the consequences of their mistakes can extend well beyond a bad answer,” said Dr. Squire. “The people building them have a responsibility to understand how they can fail and who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before that harm happens.”

Related:Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, But Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

The taxonomy reflects how the risks themselves are changing. It used to be a criminal going after a person directly, but now AI sits in the middle, which adds new players and new ways for things to go wrong. An assistant acting on someone’s behalf can be manipulated into doing damage, and a chatbot can mislead with complete confidence. Underneath, the trouble often starts in how an AI handles instructions and memory, or in the other services it’s connected to.

The research currently maps 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, with 24 defenses designed to address risks at different points. Examples range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information or acting on outdated context. It also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content an AI system processes, potentially influencing what an agent does or what a chatbot tells a user.

One of the framework’s central findings is that responsibility for preventing AI harm is spread across several parties. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person’s own device. Others have to be dealt with further upstream, by the companies that build AI products and the systems behind them, including how an AI remembers things and which other services it connects to. Sorting out which is which makes it clear where a defense belongs and who has to build it. It also undercuts the idea that people can stay safe on their own just by spotting suspicious content or double-checking what an AI tells them.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

This question of who’s responsible gets more urgent as AI moves from producing information to acting on it. A chatbot that gets an answer wrong can mislead someone, but at least that person is part of the exchange. An agent with access to a person’s accounts and the services linked to them can cause real consequences without that kind of back-and-forth. Protections need to be built around what these systems actually do, which starts with understanding how the two differ.

This research is part of a wider effort at F-Secure to build trust into the AI era. F-Secure Trust, announced alongside a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, is the company’s work on protecting people in a world where AI agents increasingly act for them. TrustGuard is designed to help protect people during AI interactions, while TrustPath aims to secure their digital journeys from discovery to delivery. The AI Harms Taxonomy gives that work a research foundation by spelling out the risks the protections need to address, and it makes clear that meaningful safeguards also depend on the companies building and running AI systems.

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Today’s digital threats go far beyond just scams. F-Secure’s Illuminate Research team studies people and technology as they actually interact, exploring the messy realities of trust, deception, and online resilience in the AI era.

The AI Harms Taxonomy is available on the Illuminate Research Hub.

F-Secure is a human-first, AI-powered consumer cyber security experience company with 38 years of expertise in tackling digital threats. We help digital service providers turn trust into a high-value growth engine — protecting their customers while enabling them to live their best digital lives in a world of relentless, AI-driven scams. With billions of digital interactions secured each year, tens of millions of consumers protected globally, and over $10bn in partner value created, we deliver proven impact at scale.

#10082. [$] Added indirection allows for larger BPF programs

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

#10081. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#10080. Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Forks of the open source Artex framework, along with 45 similar pen-testing tools, remain capable of executing credential attacks and cloud breaches at machine speed across multiple industries.

AI penetration-testing tool Artex has proven to be a boon for threat actors large and small, taking familiar attacker playbooks and deploying them at machine speeds — ushering in a potentially new era for defenders looking to get ahead of AI-enabled threats.

In July, independent developer Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. It is, by intention, a legitimate tool. However, as is so often the case with pen-test tools (such as, famously, Cobalt Strike), threat actors found a way to take advantage of it for malicious use. By late summer and early fall, a range of threat actors were using it as part of their toolkit.

Artex is capable of brute-forcing passwords, dumping databases, enumerating and abusing APIs, and more. This positions it for credential compromise and lateral movement in its own right, but the agentic element means Artex can operate at inhuman speeds. Microsoft saw an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes, for example.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in Two Days

Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, tells Dark Reading that while legitimate tool misuse is a known quantity, AI reduces the effort and expertise required to execute complex attacks. "What is particularly noteworthy about the Artex campaigns is the acceleration in speed, coordination, and autonomy," he says. "Activities that previously required deliberate integration can now be chained together and executed with limited hacking skills."

At the end of October, Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository due to rampant abuse, but many forks of the tool remain, so the threat remains. But even if all the forks went offline and Artex was no longer a going concern, the underlying threat of frameworks like it is far from over.

GitGuardian yesterday, for instance, detailed 45 different agentic attack frameworks (Artex "siblings" as the researchers called them) that are all capable of conducting attacks autonomously with the help of an AI model. Depending on the tool, these pen-testing frameworks are capable of end-to-end attacks against a network, Web application targeting, and/or autonomous coding. Some even include built-in command-and-control functionality. That's not to say these tools are inherently bad — pen-testing tools have many legitimate use cases — but it does illustrate the wide range of options for today's attacker.

The best-known incident to date involved China's Storm-0940, which adapted Artex source code into its own offensive infrastructure. Last month, around Oct. 10, the actor used the Artex framework to launch a massive password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 specific user accounts at eight critical organizations, making more than 151,000 authentication requests in the process. On average, this represented 2,900 attempts per minute without triggering automated lockout or alert.

Related:Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

When this largely failed, Storm-0940 pivoted to target ConnectWise's internal infrastructure. Attackers exfiltrated trusted OAuth application credentials belonging to ConnectWise's Cloud Backup application, allowing them to compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting.

Abuse extends far beyond a single threat actor or objective. Microsoft last week published a blog post discussing how a financially motivated Cambodia-based threat cluster tracked as Storm-3358 started using Artex in its attacks against financial organizations primarily (but not exclusively) in Southeast Asia. Microsoft said it observed Storm-3358 using Artex in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public Internet, exploit vulnerabilities, and install open source remote access Trojans (RATs).

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

Microsoft added that other threat actors have used Artex agents "to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in Web applications, use Web shells for persistence on compromised Web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration."

CrowdStrike on Oct. 29 connected Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda, India's CERT (CERT-In) tracked a financially motivated threat actor hitting financial institutions, and as of Nov. 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments. That said, because Internet exposure is not required for use, Censys estimated actual global use to be higher.

Recent Artex activity stands out because much of the story involves things security practitioners have seen time and time again. Pen-test tool abuse, nation-state tooling moving downstream to financially motivated attackers, password spraying, supply chain attacks, AI — it's a threat intelligence greatest hits album. But Guillaume Valadon, head of cybersecurity research at GitGuardian, tells Dark Reading what stands out to him most is the fast pace of attacks and the agent's initiative to accomplish the user's goals.

"At GitGuardian, we wanted to see how Artex handles secrets, so we ran it in a sealed lab," he says. "Artex ships no secret scanner, yet in every run where it acted, it found eight of the nine secrets. This included an AWS key recovered from git history. The model improvises on its hunt to reach the Artex user's goals."

Matt Snyder, Aviatrix head of security operations and threat research, says he was most surprised at how, despite the sophisticated nature of Artex's framework, the operational maturity of many threat actors deploying it appears to be low (given how many hosts remain Internet-exposed).

"AI is lowering the skill floor for offensive operations without improving operational discipline. The framework may be sophisticated, but the operational security surrounding many deployments is not," Snyder says. "This creates a dangerous combination in which more people can launch capable attacks, while poor security leaves their infrastructure, tooling, and potentially victim information exposed to anyone on the Internet."

Increasing sophistication for lower-grade attackers means, as always, defenders should be ready. Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering tools like defensive honeypots, which trick attackers into thinking they netted a valuable target.

Check Point advised in a blog post last week that organizations should expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure. "Internet-facing systems should be continuously tested and hardened, with particular attention paid to weak authentication, exposed APIs, credential leakage, remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities and cloud storage permissions," the blog post read.

Censys principal security researcher Silas Cutler offered encouraging words. Because the underlying tradecraft is conventional, the fundamentals still hold, he said, "Enforce MFA, monitor your attack surface, and practice good credential hygiene."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

The talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he showed how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

To illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

The first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries new tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

The second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With new people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

The third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a plan and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

The talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

The results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

The presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

#10078. Visited links are purple

A few weeks ago Kev Quirk asked: Do you use :visited on links? â and I said to myself: No! I donât use visited linksâ¦ but why donât I use visited links?

TL;DR: Iâve gone and styled visited links, and theyâre purple.

I did a cursory five minutes of research and found Wikipedia still styles visited links (blue to purple). MDN does too. As does the GOV.UK design system â they have a special class to opt-out of the visited style. BBC News turns black links to grey, how emo.

I decided to style visited links within my

body copy. Which to be fair is most links but not the big headings on my blog index for example. I was too intimidated to turn those purple. Maybe you can give me the courage to style those too?

It looked a bit weird at first but I like the colourful additions to my blog.

WCAG 2.2 guidelines have no requirement to differentiate visited from unvisited links. Regardless, visited links should meet all the same criteria applied to any link.

Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1.

This means that a subtle contrast different in blue vs purple is not considered an accessibility failure under that rule.

Web accessibility is all about ensuring a comparable experience for all users. Nothing can be perfectly accessible though. I think this small enhancement is fine, even if not everyone can see the difference. Itâs a rare exception though. Iâm conscious that too often excuses are made to ignore UX parity. I think any higher contrast or another visual indicator would be off-putting and impede readability. Forgoing any style doesnât help anyone either. If blue and purple is good enough for those examples mentioned above, Iâm on board.

Bryce Wray commented on Kev Quirkâs blog to note that Chromium browsers introduced :visited link partitioning in 2025. I had no idea this was a thing!

What do you think, do you care about visited link styles?

I found Kev Quirkâs blog on bubbles.town. Bubbles is a charming social RSS aggregator. Itâs doing a great job at supporting small personal blogs and promoting non-toxic topics. Bubbles is far from perfect though. It probably needs a tech filter. It certainly needs more participation in comments and voting. The developer is actively working to improve the site and a community is growing, so thatâs cool to see.

I hope Bubbles can thrive and remain human. This is the web we need to bypass the dead web Google et. al. are gatekeeping. Let them wall themselves in with their slop!

All opinions are my own and not those of a large language model. Everything I write is one hundred percent human. Because I care!
