#10077. November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

While the cornucopia of CVEs this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he says via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

Tara Seals is an award-winning journalist with 25+ years of experience as a reporter, analyst, and editor in the cybersecurity, communications, and technology spaces. As managing editor, she runs the newsroom at Dark Reading, leading a team of staff writers and freelance contributors. She also heads up strategy for a variety of in-depth, multichannel news coverage initiatives.

Prior to joining Dark Reading in 2022, Tara was editor-in-chief at cybersecurity stalwart Threatpost, and prior to that, the North American news lead for Infosecurity Magazine. She also spent 13 years working for other titles at Virgo Publishing (now part of Informa TechTarget), as executive editor and editor-in-chief at publications focused on communications service providers, channel partners, and enterprise mobile and video technology. In 2026, she was awarded a regional Azbee award for her in-depth coverage of the ongoing North Korean fake worker cyber campaign.

#10075. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

#10074. N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

The RMM provider also released a hotfix as a recommended mitigation to address public exploits for the alleged zero-days, which allow for attacker takeover.

N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers who broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers are already scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates.

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

More recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody says.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he says. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise."

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least the beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

Researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or new scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools."

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody says he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

"Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he says. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#10073. Design for Understandability

This is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

There’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the big ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

Is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

Hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

The tech industry is quickly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

Because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard

So where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more important than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test

Now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”

You might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

Consider that a decade or two ago, we used to think that writing multiple tests for every public method in an API would have been infeasible. It wasn’t because we didn’t want to, or that we weren’t trying. It was because we hadn’t designed our code to make testing possible at that level. But gradually, across the software industry, we changed our practices to design for testability. Today, designing our code for testability is so ingrained into our culture that doing anything else is practically unthinkable. We can do the same for understandability, so that our code enables us to understand it better.

Our own Code Health guide makes a strong case for understandability. It says “For code to be sustainable, it must be understood. Change cannot be made unless a developer knows what the system currently provides, and what needs to change to adapt to new circumstances. As a result, key components of code health include good documentation, easy to understand error messages, and clear, simple code”

Not only is designing for understandability important, but it’s a learnable skill. It’s not some magical ability that you either have or you don’t. There are specific, concrete actions you can take to improve the understandability of your code.

I’m going to introduce you to a few of those today. Think of it as a “starter kit” for designing for understandability. We’ll also talk more about a general theme that runs through all of these practices, so that at a certain point you can find even more ways to design your code for understandability.

The ideas I’m going to show you today are not new. But they’re not taught as well as they should be, when they’re taught at all, and most of us have only a rough understanding of how to apply them. My goal today is to sharpen that understanding just a little bit, and make it just a little more practical, so we can kickstart a process of making our code more understandable over time.

So let’s get started on each of these Design for Understandability practices.

To motivate the idea, let’s ask the question: when calling a method, what behavior should you rely on?

Let’s say we have this binary search method, but its documentation is not terribly helpful (you’ve probably seen something like this before).

Binary search is reasonably well understood, but as a caller of the method, we have some questions we want to ask about this specific implementation. Such as:

The documentation doesn’t answer these questions. So what can we do?

First, we could guess. But we’ll probably be wrong.

Second, we could read the code. But that might take a long time, especially if the particular behavior we care about is buried several levels deep.

Third, we could test the code on some examples and see what happens. But just because it works a certain way on some examples doesn’t necessarily mean it works that way for all such inputs. Furthermore, even if it works that way now, there’s no guarantee that it will continue to work that way in the future.

The point is that without a clear statement of what this code is intended to do, there’s no distinction between implementation and intent. The SWE who wants to use this code has to guess at which behavior the method commits to, versus which behavior is an implementation detail that might change over time.

There are many ways to define a contract, but for the sake of this talk I’m going to define it as a formal-ish description of the observable behavior that each participant in an interaction commits to.

In the real world, a basic contract is something like “If I cook dinner, then you will wash the dishes”.

In programming, an example might be: “If the caller provides a non-negative integer n, then the square-root function returns the square root of n”

Let’s see how contracts can help us with our binary-search example.

Here’s a possible contract for this function. It says, “If the list is sorted, binarySearch returns the index of the first occurrence of t in the list, or -1 if not found. Behavior is undefined for unsorted lists.”

We can see that this contract answers the questions we asked about it:

The power of a contract is that it defines a clear boundary between the author’s intent and the implementation. The caller doesn’t have to guess at the behavior anymore: they can just read the contract, and if a specific detail of the behavior isn’t there, they will know that it’s unspecified.

In reality, this isn’t always perfect. Whether intentionally or accidentally, we still tend to end up with code that relies on implementation details rather than specified behavior. But contracts at least give us a way to minimize this behavior.

Now that we understand what a contract looks like, let’s talk about how contracts can help us reason about and understand our code better.

Suppose you just wrote a method. I’m going to draw that method as a little circle here.

I’m going to use a purple circle to stand for methods we’ve read the code for

Now, our method doesn’t live in isolation: it calls some other code.

So, you think “Okay, well, I need to understand what those do. I’m going to read the code for those methods.”

Well, those methods call other methods, and we start thinking about this, and figure out how we’re going to reason about those. And at this point you can maybe see where I’m going.

Oh no. Now we have lots and lots of code we have to read across our entire code base.

Why do we need all this reasoning just to reason about one single method? That’s all we’re trying to do! How did we get so out of control?

So, let’s back up and try again, using Design by Contract this time.

You still have to read your own code. We can’t get around this part; that’s the change we just made.

And we haven’t changed the code. It still calls those other methods.

But now, the trick is that we can read just the contract on those called methods, not the code.

And that’s it! We can stop here. We don’t need to worry about all of that other code. The contracts tell us all we need to know about calling these other two methods.

The rest of that code still exists, but we don’t have to think about it. The contract abstracts away all that other behavior that doesn’t matter to us as the caller of these two methods.

So that is the power that contracts give to us to reason about our code.

Finally, I’ll wrap up this section with a few tips for writing contracts:

First, document the behavior that you’re willing to commit to. This is usually the same as what you want your callers to rely on. For example, you probably want to document the return value of your method. But the exact human-readable text in your error messages? Not so much.

Second, describe your error handling in your contracts. A contract does not and should not be just about the happy path. If your method might go wrong in some way, tell the caller under what conditions it might go wrong, and how you’re going to signal that to the caller, whether it be through a special return value, or an exception, or something else.

Finally, keep in mind that the more callers your method has, the harder it is to change the contract. If it’s a private method used only by your team? Sure, that’s probably an easy case to change both the contract and change the callers to match. If it’s a public method on a popular framework used by hundreds of other projects? Then renegotiating the contract is a much more expensive effort, so you should evaluate the costs and benefits carefully before deciding to do that.

So that was the first element in our Design for Understandability starter kit.

Let me explain this idea with a little story.

Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, when my wife and I started working from home, we missed having free soda at work. So we got in the habit of keeping cans of Diet Coke in the fridge.

But there was a problem: we were great at taking cans out of the fridge, but not so great about putting new ones back in. So if you’re working hard and looking forward to taking a break with a nice cold beverage, it was a big disappointment to open a Coke-less fridge and resort to drinking room-temperature soda from the pantry instead.

The problem was that we hadn’t set any rules on how we retrieve Diet Coke and how we replenish the fridge.  Without any rules governing access to the fridge, we eventually got into an unwanted state: in this case, an empty fridge.

This happens in code, too. For example, let’s say you have this proto to represent a customer’s order [Note: “proto” is Google jargon for a Protocol Buffers message, similar to a JSON object]. If you receive this proto, how much do you trust that the total actually indicates the total amount on the items?

Probably not much, right? This proto could have come from any part of your code, so it’s easy to imagine that someone forgot to set that field appropriately.

Protos give you completely uncontrolled access to the underlying representation of your data. Protos are great for transferring data back and forth across the network, but they’re poorly suited to situations where you want to rule out certain states.

To solve these kinds of problems, we can use data invariants. A data invariant is a statement about a piece of data that is always true.

Data invariants are a principled way to enforce these kinds of valid states in your data. If you use them well, you can avoid a lot of bugs in your code.

Let’s see how we can use invariants to solve the Diet Coke problem, and similar problems you might come across in your own code

First, identify the invariant you want to maintain.

Ask yourself: What’s the property you want to rely on for this piece of data? Where are the places in the code where you explicitly validate and return an error if invalid? Alternatively, where do you make the assumption that it’s invalid, but you’re not actually sure?

In this case, the invariant we want is “the fridge always contains a Diet Coke”.

Second, you need to document the invariant.

It’s important to note this is a separate step. It’s one thing to have an invariant in your own head. It’s another thing to write it down so that you communicate it to everyone else who might touch this code. Not to mention that if you come back to this code months or years later, you yourself might have forgotten which exact invariant you meant to maintain.

Write it down where people will see it: probably close to the relevant data members, or maybe in a class-level comment at the top.

Third, establish the invariant at creation time. Usually this will be done in a constructor or factory method. In this case, we’re constructing the fridge with a few drinks already added.

Fourth, every time you change your the data, make sure you maintain the invariant.

This is the part my wife and I didn’t do for our fridge. What we should have done is established a rule where if you take a Diet Coke, you put another one back in the fridge to make sure there’s another for the next person.

You can maintain the invariant many ways – that part is up to you. The important thing is that you always maintain it. Without that, you have to think to yourself “Wait, are there going to be Diet Cokes in the fridge? Did I already take them out earlier? Let me go back and check all my callers to see if they did that already”. With an invariant, though, you just know: If I have a Fridge object, then it definitely has Diet Cokes, regardless of the sequence of operations that led to this point.

Finally, one last step, and this might be the hardest one: you need to maintain the invariant as the code evolves. It’s relatively easy to maintain the invariant for a single version of code. But over the weeks, months, and years, complexity will creep in, new requirements will force you to change the code, and you might accidentally break the invariant or forget you even had one.

Establish the culture on your team that maintaining invariants is just a thing you do. If you have a mental checklist of things you look for in code review, make sure that maintaining the invariants is on that checklist.

So how do data invariants help us design for understandability? Let’s first consider what we have to do when we don’t have an invariant.

Recall this representation of all the methods in your codebase, calling each other in various ways. Suppose you have a proto-based version of the fridge, and you want to know if it has any Diet Cokes in it. Because it’s a proto, you don’t have a way of knowing what state it’s in.

So, you need to check all the callers of the current method.

And you do the check, crawling across the codebase, and you find that there’s one particular case where you didn’t enforce it.

Of course you can fix these issues one at a time as they crop up, but all that searching sounds like a lot of work, right? What do you think are the chances you’re always going to find that one particular buggy spot? What are the chances that new methods added to this web of code are going to maintain that condition?

In contrast, let’s try the version with our Fridge class and its invariant.

In this case, the class has an invariant: the Fridge always has at least one Diet Coke, no matter what operations have been done previously or where we came from. By maintaining that invariant, we’ve removed the need to check what every single caller does.

This is what data invariants do for you: they let you focus on the state you’re in now, and not how you got there.

That wraps up the section on data invariants.

The final practice I want to discuss today is isolating side effects and dependencies on global state.

To motivate this idea with an example. Let’s say there’s a supermarket point-of-sales system with this method to compute sales tax. Now ask yourself: what are the inputs and outputs for this method?

Seems pretty obvious, right? It takes in a customer’s grocery order and returns the sales tax as an integer.

But that’s not the whole story. If you dig into the implementation of this method, you’ll find that it reads in a set of sales tax rates from a separate file. That’s effectively a new input channel! The code depends on that data to compute the tax just as much as it depends on the content of the grocery order itself.

And if you look further, you’ll find that the method also records the computed tax in the store’s account database for bookkeeping purposes. That’s a new output, but it’s nowhere to be found in the type signature!

So functions have two kinds of input and output: the ones that are visible in the type signature, like the order and the computed sales tax, and the ones that are hidden, like the tax rates file and the entry in the accounting database.

The hidden outputs are more commonly known as side effects. Side effects generally come in two flavors: mutation, so modifying something like a global variable or one of your input arguments, and outputs outside of your process. That would be things like database writes, remote procedure calls, printing to the console, etc.

I don’t know a common term for the hidden inputs, but I would call these dependencies on global state. Again, there are two flavors: dependency on the state of some global variable, or a dependency on the state of the system your program is running in. That’s things like permissions to access the database, the existence of a given file on the file system, and even the ability to read the system clock.

So why are these hidden inputs and outputs a problem? They make code hard to test, hard to reuse, and hard to reason about.

Hard to test because you have to make sure you have all the necessary dependencies are set up before you can even run the method in your test. And then once you do run the method, side effects often force the test to rely more on interaction verification than state verification, which can be brittle.

Hard to reuse because the code now makes assumptions about what kinds of resources you have available to you. If you need to reuse some method in another part of the codebase, but the input data needs to come from a different source, or you need to store the results in a different place, those side effects and global states are going to create a tight coupling between your computation code and the specific sources and destinations for that computation, which will make your life harder.

Hard to reason about because, by definition, these inputs and outputs are hidden! If you don’t even know that your method is making these kinds of assumptions on the system that it’s running in, then you’re going to make some faulty conclusions about how your code will behave.

Now I’m not saying all side effects or global state are bad. And I’m not saying we should all immediately switch to a pure functional programming language like Haskell.

Effects have to happen somewhere. Without side effects, computation is just the process of making a metal box hot for a little while(and even that heat is a side effect! although not usually one we care about).

But by default, we tend to sprinkle them everywhere throughout the code. Need some input? Just read the file at whatever point you happen to be at in the code. Need to store your result? Go ahead and do it 4 layers deep into your business logic.

Without a principled approach to side effects and global state, we’re constantly running into the kinds of problems we just described.

There’s a better way, which is to isolate the side effects and the dependencies on global state. Much of our code is just logic on top of the data (once we get it) and creating new data based on that. Divide your code into the computational parts on one hand, and the parts that deal with side effects and global state on the other.

There are a few common patterns for this.

One of them is Command/Query Separation. It’s a pattern where each method is either a command, which performs some side effect, or a query, which is a pure function that returns its output as the return value. But you maintain a strict separation so that no function does both of those things.

Another pattern is called “Functional Core, Imperative Shell”. This is a pattern at the architectural level. You focus the inner modules of your system on the business logic and computation, not performing side effects – this is the “functional core”. The outer modules coordinate the effects of your system with that computation, so that the complexity of the side effects is isolated to just that outer layer, and the majority of your system is simpler due to the functional purity.

As with the other two practices, side effects and global state have a big impact on how we think about code.

For example, you might be working on a method and need to delete a file. Your assumption is that it should be okay, you think no one is using it.

But then it turns out, some other part of the codebase was relying on it, and you just broke them. The code was so far away and unrelated that you didn’t even think to check there.

On the other hand, if you isolate your side effects and global state such that they only happen in a known region of the code, then you can have confidence that you really aren’t going to break anyone else.

So, those are the three starter practices for Design for Understandability: Design by Contract, Data Invariants, and Isolating Side Effects and Dependencies on Global State.

Now, I’ve presented these as independent practices, but in fact they’re not so distinct. There’s a unifying theme to them. That theme is local reasoning.

Local reasoning means you can come to conclusions about some chunk of code by looking only at that chunk of code, plus just a small amount of the neighboring code, like the specifications or contracts of the components that you directly interact with.

This is as opposed to global reasoning. That’s the kind of reasoning where to answer even a simple question, you have to read a large chunk of the codebase, because the answer could be in any method, at any level of the call stack.

The benefit of local reasoning is that it puts a hard boundary on how far you have to look in order to figure something out about your system: there’s always a limit to how far you have to search.

So let’s talk about how each of the practices we talked about enables local reasoning. You may have noticed we covered this already, but let’s review.

Design by Contract defines the expected behavior for a caller and a called method. That means that to understand what behavior a caller can rely on, or what behavior a called method is obligated to implement, the only place we need to look is the defined interface for that called method. Without that, we would revert to global reasoning to find all the parts of the code that might depend on some aspect of this method’s behavior.

Data invariants often go hand in hand with contracts, but they usually say something about an entire object rather than a single method on that object.

If you have a piece of data and you want to know something about its validity, like “does this fridge have any diet cokes?”, an invariant is what lets you immediately conclude yes, without looking at the callers that produced that data.

Finally, by isolating side effects and global state, you minimize the number of places in your code where a change in one part of the code can cause a problem in a completely unrelated part. So it lets you say things like “this is the only part of the code that’s allowed to touch this file, so I know for sure that it’s safe to delete”.

Another way of looking at local reasoning is to say that it minimizes the amount of context we need in order to reason about the system.

With global reasoning, you might need to know about any arbitrary part of your codebase, because the part that breaks your assumptions could be anywhere. You need to have the whole system loaded into your head in order to understand it.

Local reasoning keeps the amount of stuff you need loaded into your head to a reasonable size.

And guess what else benefits from small contexts: LLMs!

A key portion of making an LLM useful for your work is giving an LLM the right context to give good suggestions. But contexts costs tokens, and your tokens are limited. So LLMs give us another great motivation to use local reasoning and minimize our context.

In other words, if you want your LLMs to be useful to you, then design your systems for understandability. Keep the necessary context small to make it easier for both you and your LLM to work with your code.

At the beginning of this talk, I compared “Design for Understandability” to “Design for Testability”. I’d like to revisit that for a moment.

Before designing for testability was the norm, the default testing approach was application-level testing. Our code wasn’t set up for practices like dependency injection, so there was no way to run your code without setting up a huge set of dependencies as well. It wasn’t until we started designing and building our systems with testability in mind that we were able to make unit testing practical.

That’s how it is with understandability and local reasoning, as well. If you don’t design for it ahead of time, it’s somewhere between hard and impossible to use local reasoning. But if you design for it along the way, you can make it work.

If you’ve never heard of unit testing, then application-level testing seems obvious, and straightforward. But it’s not sufficient for modern software engineering. The same is true for global reasoning. I say it’s time we made designing for understandability a required part of our work, just like we did for testability.

So you may be thinking: that all sounds good, and these practices sound good on paper, but is designing for understandability feasible in practice? You’re probably not working in a brand-new greenfield project. You’re probably working on old code, with lots of old warts and complexity, and the situation may seem hopeless. Can you really do this?

I’m here to say yes, this is feasible, if you take it one small step at a time. I’ll share some tips for getting started.

First off, take little bits at a time. Don’t try to boil the ocean. Don’t say “We’re going to take two weeks off from our normal work, make all of our code perfectly understandable, and then we’re done!”. That’s not going to work; you’re going to have a bad time.

Instead, try applying some of these practices to just new methods that you write. You might have some old code out there that’s hard to change. So be it. Start with just the new methods and build some momentum.

Teach your teammates, as well. Maybe share this talk, or find other ways to help your teammates design for understandability.

And finally, you might consider group programming sessions where you all get together and discuss: what does designing for understandability mean in your context? The Monarch team at Google did this with their Design by Contract practice and it worked well for them.

Here are some further resources to learn more about Design for Understandability. I’m not going to go into them in detail, but please feel free to go revisit the slides after the talk and check these out.

[Public links reproduced here for the blog post:]

In conclusion: design your code for understandability. Whenever you’re working on some code and realize that you’re falling back to global reasoning, pause for a moment. Ask yourself: can I do this with local reasoning instead? Would a contract or an invariant help here? Or what if I moved the side effects and global state somewhere else? Or, maybe you’ll think of some other practice that fits here – you probably know a lot of local-reasoning practices, even if you didn’t have the terminology to call it that until today.

It’s time to make design for understandability just as much a part of software engineering as designing for testability is today. Understandability is not just helpful – it’s crucial, especially with Google-size systems. And not just that, but making your code understandable is doable if you design for it along the way.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations AI-Assisted Software Delivery: From Code to Production

The panelists explore how engineering teams adapt delivery architectures, pipelines, security, and governance for AI-assisted development. They share practical strategies for verifying AI-generated code, solving testing and deployment bottlenecks, maintaining human oversight, and measuring AI’s true impact on software velocity, quality, reliability, and operational cost.

Garima Bajpai is the Founder of the DevOps Community of Practice in Canada. Martin Reynolds is a Field CTO at Harness. Patrick Debois is an AI Product Engineer and AI Native Dev Advisor. Gunnar Grosch is a Developer Advocate at Sinch. Renato Losio is an InfoQ Staff Editor, Cloud Expert, and AWS Data Hero.

InfoQ Live is a virtual event designed for you, the modern software practitioner. Learn from extraordinary speakers driving change and innovation.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Renato Losio: Today we'll discuss how AI is changing software delivery, so from code generation to production, how AI-assisted software delivery is changing in our crazy times.

We are all familiar with AI in general now and how it's changing every aspect of our developer life, but one of the challenges we discuss maybe less is how is integrating AI into the broader engineering lifecycle while maintaining quality, security, and reliability.

My name is Renato Losio. I'm an editor at InfoQ. I'm joined today by four experts coming from different companies, different sectors, different countries. I'd like to give a chance to each one of them to introduce themselves and share their journey, and why they are part of this panel today.

I would call that our solo level, team shared level working together. Those are things that are easy to hand off, let agents do, and then you get the result back and you can take part of it. Same with the other end of the lifecycle, where you deploy, you test, you iterate, and you have that loop over and over again. Also, fairly easy to hand off to agents and let them take part of it.

What I'm still seeing a lot is that the step in between, that's still where developers or engineers are engaged. They're still doing a lot of the work in that in-between, so handing off the initial work, handing off that last leg of the work, but still doing a lot of the work in between. I think a lot of it comes down to trust, being able to actually hand off that entire work. It's a bit scary.

Renato Losio: I don't know, really on a personal experience, I can say that if you talk to many practitioners it's, yes, we are experimenting with it. We are doing that. Martin Reynolds: I think that's something that comes up quite often, especially work with quite a lot of regulated environments, and the trust is a big thing. The mechanism might not be exactly the same, but I think you need the governance set up the same way, so that they should have things like scoped credentials, policies, approvals, audit trail, so they're not free-roaming agents. Coming back to that gap that was mentioned, it's interesting, because I think you're right. Garima Bajpai: I actually wanted to add a few things here, because, again, as Patrick and Gunnar alluded to the fact that with AI, the individual productivity has improved.
