#10062. Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The CCP built a Big Data system to scrape reams of information and learn about individuals abroad, to potentially target and exploit them. Think Alice Huang Lite.

The Chinese government is keeping tabs on ethnic Chinese people abroad via an AI-powered Big Data mining program. In some cases, the program is helping the government design influence operations targeting high-ranking individuals in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

Since the AI boom began, world leaders have been feeling out how to exploit it to cement their power. While Washington's emphasis has been on shorter-term AI ventures — tracking immigrants and political protestors, identifying social services to cut, etc. — the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has been building something more durable: a data center that facilitates gargantuan Web scraping from social media and other public sources, feeds the results into machine learning algorithms, and outputs actionable intelligence for the apparatchiks in Beijing.

That's according to documents leaked to China watchdog NetAskari. In a report shared with Dark Reading and Sky News UK ahead of publication, NetAskari detailed a program that balances straightforward government PR with unsavory surveillance. Sometimes the data gathering has been designed around Cambridge Analytica-style targeted propaganda campaigns. In more nefarious cases, it has been used to identify individuals in political and economic spheres of interest who might one day make good spies or unwitting assets in spy campaigns.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

"A foreign nation with rather undemocratic tendencies is running an extensive, AI-charged analysis and information-scraping operation to find ways to influence other nations' internal social, economic, and political landscapes," a NetAskari analyst explains in an interview with Dark Reading over Signal. "That this system is particularly aiming at the Chinese diaspora, to see if [foreign citizens] can be used to further these ambitions, even if they might not be aware of it, is rather shocking."

On Nov. 8, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang — one of the few most important people in the most important industry in the world — emailed his staff, admitting to an affair with a newly outed spy. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) agent, Alice Huang, redirected Nvidia semiconductors to China, where they're banned, and translated intelligence from the CEO to the CCP.

While the MSS ran Huang, the United Front Work Department (UFWD) took its own, less dramatic approach to the challenge of breaching Taiwan's semiconductor industry.

The UFWD's main game is influence operations, at home and abroad, according to NetAskari. Its mission includes gauging and shaping media narratives about China abroad, engaging Chinese diaspora communities — to their benefit or detriment, depending on the situation — and, in certain cases, attempting to gain influence over powerful or otherwise useful individuals and organizations in China and abroad.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

In this instance, the UFWD appears to have been scoping out ethnic Chinese individuals involved in the semiconductor industry. A leaked report titled "Profiles of Ethnic-Chinese Leading Talent in the Chip Field, Their Circle Characteristics, and Work Recommendations" identifies executives of the Taiwanese AI company Skymizer, high-performing students at a top Taiwanese research university, and an AI research center director at Microsoft, among others, as individuals of note. It then details strategies for getting closer to these VIPs, like "leverage non-official organizations — hometown associations, alumni associations, professional societies — for relationship-building and cooperation."

The system used to generate this report is called the "Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform."

The platform's brain is a 500-square-meter Big Data laboratory at Jinan University in Guangzhou, built to comfortably house rows of server racks and at least 100 employees.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Basically, it's built to ingest massive amounts of online information about overseas Chinese communities, identify people, relationships, and public sentiments, and convert it all into actionable reports for CCP leadership, according to NetAskari.

Social media provides much of the content. The platform scrapes liberally from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and X, plus Chinese platforms like Weibo and WeChat. As a rule, the actual scrapers are run on machines located in foreign countries. As with Chinese hacking campaigns more broadly, the machines doing the crimes are also shielded behind rotating proxy networks. The goal of this obfuscation, one leaked document explains, is to “ensure the security of data collection and prevent the collection system from being traced and discovered" by targeted platforms.

The data then makes its way to China for processing. Foreign languages are translated into Chinese, keywords are extracted, and meaningful links are drawn. UFWD then cross-references these data with preexisting records of notable people identified as being involved in the media, sciences, politics, etc., as well as blacklisted and "two-faced people." These two sources feed a "business system" — the layer that seems to draw meaningful connections about public sentiments, the results of influence operations, and more.

Sometimes, the final reports outputted by this multitiered system simply concern public relations trends. Sometimes they've been used to identify ethnic Chinese individuals of note around the world — be they Taiwanese engineers, social media influencers, or something in between — and unearth strategies for how to utilize them to further the ends of the Chinese Communist Party.

Overall, the NetAskari analyst describes the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform as "a worldwide dragnet that uses open source intelligence (OSINT) and Big Data analysis to identify and find potential collaborators, partners, and affiliates that the UFWD can work with to further their goal [of] extending the Communist Party's influence abroad and creating a 'China-friendly' environment in other nations' political, economic, and social settings."

It's nothing the UFWD wasn't doing before, to be sure. Instead, the analyst adds, "What used to be done manually, at a much slower speed, is now supercharged via AI and modern technology."

That, ultimately, is the rub. The leaked documents contain only outdated references, from 2021, about how machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms fit into this picture. It's unclear whether, and how, more modern large language models have been incorporated into — and potentially supercharged — the system. The better the AI gets, the more wide-ranging and granular the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform can become, with real consequences for people who may not know they are being targeted by a foreign nation.

"A surveillance state can't accept that its own citizens are escaping to other nations, outside the reach of Beijing's grasp. For the best part of the last 20 years, most people had the luxury to ignore this part of the Chinese state. Often practical and physical limitations restricted Chinese organiations to expand too quickly abroad or even get a foothold. But with remote methods like the ones we have seen applied in the Big-Data center of Jinan University, these 'natural boundaries' don't apply anymore," the analyst laments.

"Pair it now with ever-growing globalization, China's stepping out onto the world stage, and crises of democracy in many Western nations, and it is not hard to see why such operations should concern even average citizens in the US or Europe," he says. "Even if they have no personal ties to China."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10061. AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents

A monthly overview of things you need to know as an architect or aspiring architect.

QCon AI New York (December 15-16, 2026): Learn how senior engineers are building AI systems that hold up in production. Register Now

Facilitating the Spread of Knowledge and Innovation in Professional Software Development

Unlock the full InfoQ experience by logging in! Stay updated with your favorite authors and topics, engage with content, and download exclusive resources.

In this episode, Christopher "CRob" Robinson, CTO of OpenSSF, Akrites and Chief Security Architect of the Linux Foundation, explores the state of software supply chain security amid multiple security incidents and explains how tools like Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework, and SLSA help harden software.

Jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce.

Nicholas Matsakis shares why AI makes Rust the ideal choice for modern production systems, skipping steep adoption hurdles via compiler guardrails. He discusses Symposium - an open-source, agent-oriented toolchain from the Rust Foundation - and demonstrates how the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) standardizes agent-to-tool extensibility across diverse enterprise developer workflows.

Henry Wilson shares actionable tools from the BBC Sounds re-architecture to help senior engineering leaders drive technical strategy. He discusses building buy-in, navigating active resistors, using RFCs and ADRs, and balancing tradeoffs - showing that effective software architecture is fundamentally about communication, relationship-building, and organizational influence.

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents

Nov 20, 2026 6 min read

AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local implementation of more than 200 of its services dedicated to the public domain under CC0, and says that "thousands of autonomous AI agents wrote every line of code" in it. As InfoQ reported at launch, it ships as a single Rust binary generated from AWS's 438 public API models and listens on port 9297. The week since has brought the first independent fidelity numbers and a divided practitioner reaction.

Pointing an existing SDK, CLI, or coding agent at the emulator is a matter of environment variables, after which the launch post by Daniel Abib says, "your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do":

The same shell serves an agent. In the post, Kiro is asked to create and read back a DynamoDB table and issues the ordinary CLI calls against the local endpoint:

Matt Wood, AWS's chief AI and technology officer, argues that the loop matters because of what an agent does while a check is slow: "A coding agent can build a lot of software around an incorrect assumption." He also names the failure mode an emulator introduces:

An agent learns from the environment it experiences. If the emulator accepts behavior that AWS rejects, training can reinforce a mistake. An agent might also discover a shortcut that succeeds only because of an emulator defect.

The fidelity scores exist to expose that gap: each release publishes per service how many tests pass out of how many were verified against real AWS, with the failing tests public too, and Abib asks readers to "read a score as a snapshot of a product that's improving."

Senior principal engineer Matthew Goldberg traces the project to a three-line prompt given to Kiro, "the simplest prompt that I could think of without any expectation that this would work":

Kiro came back after 15 minutes with a passable first version of an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). I refined my prompt and had Kiro build me the rest of AWS over the weekend. And it did. It obviously had gaps, but it was compelling enough that my team started using it to test our software that Monday.

The production version is built by three agent teams: "One team manages a test suite; one team finds issues in the emulator; and one team fixes those issues." Each fix must pass a gate that compiles the change and runs agent reviews for coding standards, security, and fidelity regression. "Our team hasn't written or reviewed any of the code," Goldberg writes, and describes what the gate carries:

If any of those checks fail, the change is sent back to the agent for rework; if they all pass, it is merged to mainline. We've seen thousands of issues fixed every day as hundreds of agents concurrently work on the codebase. Without this merge gate, we wouldn't trust what our agents are building.

Swami Sivasubramanian, in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog, recalls rebuilding a replication engine with Kiro that had taken his team four months by hand:

I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours

In his telling, the engineer's job becomes "to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct."

The first measurements from outside AWS come from Kento Ikeda, an AWS Community Builder, who ran version 1.0.322 in GitHub Actions the day after launch. DynamoDB, S3 and SQS passed roughly 60 to 70 percent of their fidelity tests at service level and 80 to 100 percent on the operations its code called, while CloudFormation sat near 20 percent. The emulator matched AWS's error wording, but a new DynamoDB table stayed in CREATING for three seconds and rejected writes until then. "Being generated from API models only means the shape of requests and responses matches AWS," he writes, and places the tool between mocks and a real sandbox as a third layer rather than a replacement for either.

The launch post draws its hardest line at security:

Don't use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn't evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501, telemetry is on by default, throttling, outages and regional differences are not simulated, and the repository does not accept pull requests. On Hacker News, one reader quoted the line on the security page that the emulator "never denies a request signed with its own key" and asked why IAM was left out:

I think because the agents were only building on the public API surface, it's hard to build this part. But they should've tried and let the agents read whatever policy engines AWS has. Or maybe it's a way to prevent someone from trivially running aws-emulator as AWSaaS?

The thread's first question was whether this was "just an exercise or a real product they are going to ship and maintain," answered by a commenter identifying as AWS staff with "It's a real product that we plan to maintain." Another counted "29,684 commits in a repository less than a month old" and said it "does not instill confidence." On r/aws, the most-upvoted comment turned Amazon's own line around, calling agents that fix code "without human review" a terrible idea for a tool used to test before production. The reply was that the API specifications already exist and the SDKs are generated from them, so a server derived from a fixed contract is where agents can iterate until the tests pass.

The timing matters to the people in those threads. LocalStack's free Hobby plan now requires an account and prohibits commercial use, with paid seats from $39 a month, and several commenters had already moved to Floci. One of them put the AWS release in that context:

But in the wake of Localstack's changes, the landscape has been full of slopware and low trust anyway. I don't think this is worse, for now at least.

AWS's version costs nothing and can be forked by either project. Sivasubramanian says AWS "will share more about this work at re:Invent" in December.

#10059. Removing binder.c

Every article on LWN.net is written for humans, by humans. If you've enjoyed this article and want to see more like it, your subscription goes a long way to keeping the slop at bay. We are offering a free one-month trial subscription (no credit card required) to get you started.

The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas announced that he had deleted the C code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas said, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices. Its design originated in BeOS, but it has grown significantly since then. It provides a rich set of operations for allowing processes to communicate with the minimum amount of overhead. It also, therefore, presents a large attack surface for Android. Many complicated chained attacks against Android have involved Binder at one step or another, Llamas explained. Google's internal "red team" (the team dedicated to proactive security research) deemed Binder to be the most vulnerability-dense component in the entire operating system, with more CVEs per line than anywhere else.

That made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas said. Binder was the first user of Rust in the kernel, he added, although Ryhl did not publicly post the first version of what became the Rust implementation until 2023, well after the Rust experiment started in 2021. All told, the effort took more than five years. Binder is used for every single screen touch, permission check, and cross-application message on Android, which runs on more than three billion devices. In total, it works out to hundreds of billions of Binder transactions per second, globally, he added. That scale meant that even the smallest discrepancy between the interface provided by the C version and the one provided by the Rust version would cause problems and regressions for some use case.

One particularly tricky aspect has been performance, Ryhl said. Throughput doesn't matter that much; what matters is the tail latencies. Most screen frames on Android have a Binder transaction in the critical path of the frame, she explained. So, a difference of two microseconds on average is not a real problem, but if Binder is ever twenty milliseconds slower, even once in a while, people will notice and care.

The actual algorithms that the C and Rust implementations use are identical, she continued, so there are no large differences in throughput. But, because Rust handles locking differently, there were problems with the tail latency from lock contention that she had to debug. For example, one user-reported traceback showed Binder attempting to take a mutex that was held by another process. That process was preempted, and did not resume executing for twenty milliseconds, well past the sixteen millisecond budget to render a single frame.

It was a classic case of priority inversion. To solve the problem in Binder, Ryhl moved as many operations out from under the lock as possible, and was able to replace it with a spinlock, which made the problem go away. The equivalent lock in the C implementation was already a spinlock: "I deviated from C Binder, and pow. It has eighteen years of accumulated quirks."

Eventually, however, the Rust implementation was good enough for most use cases. And the C implementation was still producing new vulnerabilities every time someone tried to introduce a new feature. Eventually, Llamas and Ryhl decided to only add new features to the Rust implementation, in order to motivate people to switch and to avoid headaches from the C implementation. That policy has resulted in the Rust version becoming faster than the C version, because Ryhl was able to introduce an algorithmic improvement that reduced the number of needed system calls, a change that had been considered too complex for the C implementation. Now that the C implementation has been deleted, there are more of those coming, she promised.

Another area that proved difficult was dealing with tracepoints. Users aren't supposed to rely on the presence or behavior of most kernel-internal tracepoints, but they do. This meant that Ryhl had to copy the existing tracepoints in Binder as a de facto part of the driver's API. That even extended into some of the data structures involved in the driver. In one case, she said, there was a reference-counted structure that had a slightly different reference count in the Rust implementation, because the Rust code was holding an additional pointer to the structure. That turned out to be a problem for one particular piece of client code, since it relied on checking the reference count via a tracepoint in order to determine when the C implementation had reached a particular state.

There was also a lot of toolchain support needed, Ryhl continued. The Rust implementation had to work with kernel address-space layout randomization (KASLR), control-flow integrity (CFI), and profile-guided optimization. Production Android kernels are built with all of those enabled, and since they impact code generation, the Rust code needed to account for them.

Llamas then went into more detail about the deployment plan that will be used to convert users to the Rust implementation. A major problem with just rolling the Rust implementation out is the existence of vendor hooks: custom tracepoints used to inject vendor-specific behavior into the kernel. The Rust implementation of Binder was not able to reproduce those in every case, and therefore many vendors are stuck on the C implementation until they update their code. That's going to be a slow process.

Old stable versions of the kernel will continue to have the C Binder, and receive security fixes, which gives the various Android vendors a little bit of leeway until they're forced to update. After the conference, the patch removing the C implementation was merged as part of the 7.4 merge window, so that is the version past which the Rust implementation is required. 7.3 is the designated long-term-support release for 2026.

One person asked whether this would pose a problem for people compiling the kernel with GCC. Miguel Ojeda responded that many distributions are using a workaround for the current lack of Rust support in GCC: they are building the C side of the kernel with GCC, and the Rust side with LLVM. He said that he had advised against compiling the kernel in that way, because it is "a complete hack", though people who use it are unlikely to complain about being forced onto Clang. Greg Kroah-Hartman added that it will take months or years to learn about anyone who has problems with the Rust version of the driver, given how slowly Android vendors update their kernels. Furthermore, the removal is a single patch that can be cleanly reverted, if someone needs to continue using the C version.

Llamas thought that it was worth considering what the removal process should look like for other code that gets ported to Rust. He asked what people thought should happen to the C version of converted drivers on long-term-support branches. Ojeda said that the process would be exactly the same as the existing policy for replaced C code. The only difference between Rust and C in long-term-support releases is that the Rust maintainers backport fixes for soundness problems, he said. Kroah-Hartman told Llamas not to worry about code that has been replaced: "Just delete it. I take patches for subsystems that have been deleted. It's fine."

With that declaration, the session, the conference, and the presence of the C Binder driver in the kernel were all over. Binder is the first nontrivial component in the kernel to be ported to Rust, and its journey has revealed several pitfalls that don't apply to new drivers written in Rust from scratch. Still, the most difficult problems were not Rust-specific; they were the compatibility problems that any rewrite would face. Whether any other kernel components will find the hassle of a rewrite worth it, and how long they will take to accomplish it, remains to be seen.

[ Thanks to the Linux Foundation, LWN's travel sponsor, for supporting my travel to Kangrejos. ]

This isn't a workaround, it's entirely normal. The C ABI is the same between GCC and LLVM. The only downside I'm aware of is that you can't do cross-language LTO this way.

For the (large) subset of things that are standardized and ABI-defined, yes, but if there's e.g. an __attribute__((packed)) on a struct, using the same version of clang for your C compiler and for bindgen (in the form of libclang) can be expected to get it right, and there is no such expectation if it's two different compilers. And of course if you do something like enable a layout-changing plugin in GCC like randstruct, then this will definitely not work (though Kconfig prevents that particular mistake).

It's equivalent to the reason that the standard advice is to use the exact same compiler for your kernel itself and for kernel modules. The ABI is supposed to be standard, but the kernel uses lots of language features and compiler-specific features.

(To be clear, I'm inclined to agree with you that it will generally work, and for over 20 years there has not actually been any enforcement that you did use the same compiler version.)

Aren't there codegen-affecting flags like CFI and such that are build options in the kernel? I imagine that needs compiler internal logic to match…

Aren't there codegen-affecting flags like CFI and such that are build options in the kernel? I imagine that needs compiler internal logic to match…

Codegen-affecting, yes, but are they ABI-affecting?

CFI is probably relaxed around anything that looks like an global-visibility symbol. What are other codegen-affecting options that involve nontrivial internal logic?

Other distributions like RHEL and SLES don't either. Is there a particular reason to single out Google here?

I just bought a Samsung A27 (not a flagship), and Samsung promises 6 OS upgrades and 6 years of security updates. In this case (and probably others) the clock starts to run when a smartphone model appears globally, so it certainly is a good idea to look at the release year when comparing the update promises of different smart phones.

If I search for 6 years of security updates, my favourite price comparison site lists smartphones from CMF, Honor, Motorola, Nothing, OnePlus, Oppo, Realme, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Xiaomi, so it's not just Samsung flagships. If you ask for 7 years instead, you get a different set of manufacturers (including Google); for 8 years, you get Fairphone. No one promises 9 or 10 years of security updates.

I previously had a Moto G100, gifted one year after it was released; it only had one more major Android release update, and security fixes (which were already dripping at glacial pace) probably have finished too by now...

#10058. Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.

A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.

The attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands and rapidly broke through the retailer's defenses. The attacker ultimately harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes.

Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. That said, the timing was such that investigators believe this activity was "more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent."

The security firm said this incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Symantec has investigated since May, though it added that activity was heavily concentrated around September.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in Two Days

Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine speed.

In this attack specifically, Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing more on the timeline it was able to glean from its post-incident investigation. According to the blog post, the attacker worked at first by hand, which investigators determined due to artifacts like typing errors.

When every staged payload was terminated by security software, indicators suggest attacker tactics changed when they tried again the next day. "For almost two hours," Symantec said, "the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections and, in places, comments that read as a model's reasoning." Approximately 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, attackers managed to laterally move to a second server.

The blog post hypothesizes that the attackers behind the attack were likely financially motivated, as they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and one address they contacted was linked to an operation that stole card data from online retailers.

Related:Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

During the second-stage activity, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to the SolarWinds Orion monitoring software. And while the idea of AI speeding up or improving attacker tradecraft is nothing new, the attack is its deployment of AI to a hands-on keyboard attack in progress and possibly seizing victory out of an apparent defeat. It presents LLMs as a difference-maker for a less skilled threat actor.

Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession.

"The retry pattern is a signal itself," he says. "Blocking on behavior rather than file names or exact commands matters much more. Treating a blocked attempt followed by a variant as a high-priority alert is worth considering."

Although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still important, but it can’t be the only countermeasure."

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

#10057. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#10056. Extortion Group Luna Moth Flits Into Law Firms a Second Time

The cybercriminals are retargeting law firms that refused to pay its first ransom, with a social engineering con aimed at stealing Microsoft access tokens.

A data extortion outfit has returned to previously targeted law firms for a second go, via a "vishing"-based social engineering campaign where they purport to be IT staff.

That's according to the ReliaQuest Threat Research team, which today published a blog post disclosing that Luna Moth, a threat extortion group that has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023, has for now abandoned remote-management tools and manual exfiltration to steal data, instead looking to swindle victims out of access tokens. Then, they're using these tokens to access and steal information.

Joseph Keyes, author of the blog post and cyber threat intelligence analyst at ReliaQuest, wrote that this latest wave of targets are "likely" those that didn't pay Luna Moth's first extortion demand, with this second hit coming weeks-to-months later.

A ReliaQuest spokesperson tells Dark Reading that these firms were targeted a second time because the group knows these organizations can be socially engineered (so it tries again with different tactics), for a second set of data. Moreover, as fewer organizations are paying, law firms make a good fit to target, because "their client data is highly sensitive and the reputational hit from exposure is severe, so repeated leverage is worth the effort."

Related:3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

In the initial variants of the attack, Luna Moth would reach out as IT support and trick victims into connecting to Windows' built-in remote assistance tool. It would then download data directly. This time, the group sent blank-subject emails from a free email address with a broken PDF masquerading as a business report; the "report" would then fail to open. The attacker would use this pretext to reach out soon after, posing as IT support responding to a malicious alert, while at the same time offering to fix the PDF.

Once on a video call, the "IT support" directs the target to turn on screen-share functionality so they can direct the target through a "fix." The attacker then tells the target to open Microsoft Copilot from the Web browser on their work laptop, open the browser's developer tools, find the request Copilot sends to Microsoft Graph, and copy the application's access token.

The attacker instructs the target to paste the token into a public text-sharing site the attacker can access. Finally, the attacker gives the token to its own folder and downloads files through the Microsoft Graph API.

This social engineering tactic requires no malware and no vulnerability. It relies solely on tricking a target into giving an access token, effectively a master key into the front door of an organization. The use of IT support to "fix" a technical issue evokes ClickFix, as both techniques rely on human problem-solving tendencies to trick an end user.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

The ReliaQuest spokesperson says the firm considers this attack representative of a gap in how controls are scoped within an organization. Because the token is issued to the victim's compliant device and handed over "willingly," security red flags do not go off.

"A token is a bearer credential, so it works from anywhere until it expires, unless CAE [Continuous Access Evaluation] with strict location enforcement (or token binding) applies," the spokesperson says. "Similar to device code phishing, the user completes a legitimate flow, so MFA is satisfied. The weakness is the assumption that authentication equals ongoing trust. Microsoft's defaults, such as the 60- to 90-minute lifetime and CAE not being enforced by default, make it easier."

ReliaQuest recommends that organizations turn CAE on by default, block browser developer tools and token-inspection pages on managed browsers, and restrict remote-support and screen-sharing tools where there's no business need. Additionally, it may be wise to inform employees of the ways threat actors attempt to steal credentials from employees.

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

As the blog post put it, "Tell users that IT will never ask for developer tools or tokens and that they should verify IT requests by callback."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

InfoQ Homepage Articles Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover

Nov 20, 2026 16 min read

I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title. The conditions were all there. I just hadn't looked at them as a system that would eventually fail, only as infrastructure that had been working fine so far. My team owned a Terraform execution platform. The registry was backed by S3, which is standard stuff. Nothing else exotic was added. One morning the dashboard lit up, showing registry failures and artifacts not downloading. We declared an incident and started the usual process of elimination.

Two hours into our investigation, I was still convinced we had done something wrong. Perhaps we had a misconfigured bucket policy or added a permissions boundary incorrectly. Hopefully, this problem was  embarrassingly fixable. I kept going back to our changes, our config, and our code. The problem wasn't in any of those places.

The actual cause took hours to surface. S3 signed URLs worked fine. You could manually call one and download an artifact without issue. But Terraform calls those URLs in sequence. When it resolves module dependencies, it fires a bunch of them back-to-back. Some of those requests were silently failing. Not all of them failed and not  in any consistent pattern, just... some, which was enough, to break the pipeline. From every dashboard we viewed, it looked like a registry bug, rather than an S3 bug.

Microsoft Ignite 2026; Explore What's Next in AI and Software Engineering - Learn how to architect agentic systems, modernize cloud infrastructure, and tackle emerging engineering challenges. Get practical insights from Microsoft experts and industry leaders. Microsoft Ignite is less than two weeks away! Register now to join us in person or attend online for free, November 17–20.

We found the real cause by building a controlled test environment on my laptop. The failures were intermittent and appeared only in production, where experimenting is discouraged, so I needed a safe way to reproduce them. I wrote a small Terraform configuration that downloads modules from our registry, the same path our pipelines use, and ran it under a load test. I also checked out the Terraform source and added logging for HTTP request and response headers. Logging exposed an easy-to-miss detail. Terraform hands module downloads to HashiCorp's go-getter library, which sends a HEAD request to each signed URL before the GET, to check whether the download can be resumed. The load test reproduced the failure within ten minutes; the logs traced it to that HEAD request rather than to our registry. I proposed that a recent change in how AWS handled the HEAD request was producing the downstream 404.

This hypothesis was initially not obvious even to their support personnel. I substantiated it with clear reproduction steps and diagnostic evidence. After they escalated internally to their architecture team, they confirmed that a recent change in request handling was the root cause and rolled back the change, restoring expected behavior. The lesson I took from this situation was when a managed dependency fails intermittently, reproduce your client's exact call pattern outside of production and instrument the client, not just the server.

Detection took a few hours. Recovery took nearly twenty-four hours, most of which was spent on support calls proving the issue was on their end waiting for AWS to acknowledge other customers were affected and waiting for the rollback to ship. Once AWS rolled back the S3 deployment, concurrent signed URL requests stabilized and the registry recovered without any changes on our end.

The mechanism here, signed URLs, concurrency, isn't the important part. The important part is the assumption I had been running on without examining it, that cloud infrastructure is reliable by default. That 99.99 percent is essentially "always works". I had treated the SLA like a guarantee rather than a statistical claim about a distribution with a tail I just hadn't seen yet.

Fifty-two minutes and thirty-six seconds of downtime per year. Considering the scale at which we were operating, hitting that window was not a matter of if, because I already had and more than once. I just hadn't treated it as evidence that my design needed to change.

Every organization I have worked for has made the same mistake and I bet that yours has too. Someone builds an observability system early on. They care about it. The dashboards are thoughtful, the alerts are calibrated, and the runbooks are linked. Then the system grows, engineers move on, haphazardly adding and wiring  in new services without anyone updating what came before. The people who built the original dashboards aren't around to update them and the people who are around are nervous to touch something they didn't build and don't fully understand. Alerts drift out of calibration and dashboards start showing issues nobody on the current team knows how to interpret.

Then something breaks at a bad hour and the person on call opens Grafana and spends twenty minutes just trying to figure out what they are seeing. I have been in that position. The problem runs deeper than knowledge. It is a design failure, not a skills gap. The dashboards were built as a reporting layer, something that shows you what is happening. But they were never connected to anything that does something about what is happening. The human is still the bridge between signal and response.

The mistake has nothing to do with tooling choice, query language, or dashboard layout. The mistake is treating observability as a way to inform humans rather than a way to drive system behavior. The difference is significant in practice. In reporting, a human receives an alert, interprets it under stress at a bad hour, decides what to do, and acts. In a control plane, the system receives and evaluates the signal against a defined policy, acts, and tells the human what happened. One of those scales with your headcount and on-call rotation, while the other breaks the moment both are stretched thin.

None of the tooling required for this design is new. Prometheus has had alerting rules and webhook routing for years. Terraform can reconfigure routing weights. The components all exist; they just haven't been wired together with automation as the explicit goal. The pattern is the same at every scale, from pod autoscaling to regional failover: observe, decide, act, and confirm.

I have run Prometheus and Grafana stacks across hundreds of services, large builds and deployment pipelines, with thousands of executions per day. These tools are powerful but carry an operational cost teams consistently underestimate. Consider that expertise concentrates. When the person who really knows the stack leaves, calibration drifts silently until something breaks at the worst possible moment. Treat your observability stack with the same ownership model as your production services with regular reviews, real failure testing, and collective ownership that does not expire when the original author leaves.

Figure 1. Observability as a reporting layer vs. a control plane.The difference is whether a human or the system bridges signal to response. (Source: created by author.)

I have never worked with anyone who needed a whitepaper to understand why multi-region matters. Instead, they needed an outage. After a major regional failure hit one of our cloud providers, the conversation about moving the Terraform registry to active-active architecture happened. The registry is called during every pipeline execution: every build, every deployment, and every release. When it goes down, every build, every deployment, and every release across every team stops with it. The blast radius of that dependency is much larger than it looks on an architecture diagram; it took a real outage for that to land viscerally for everyone involved.

We chose active-active, not active-passive. The reason for this choice comes up less often in architecture discussions than it should. We wanted the secondary region under real production load before we needed it for failover.

Active-passive looks good in diagrams. The failure mode is subtle and tends to surface at the worst possible time. The passive region has never handled your actual traffic. Its configuration has drifted unnoticed. Caches are cold and downstream dependencies haven't been exercised under anything close to real load. You have tested it in staging, maybe, with synthetic load that doesn't match your real traffic profile. When you fail under pressure, during an active incident with people watching, you discover all of these issues simultaneously.

I have been on that incident bridge. It is a specific kind of unpleasantry. You are trying to recover from one problem while discovering a second set of problems you didn't know you had. Active-active costs more. You have to keep regions in sync. Data consistency under partition requires careful thought. But when a region degrades, you shift load in a system that has been running in two regions all along, not making a leap of faith into an untested environment. We ran 50/50 under normal operation, which gave us continuous validation. Both regions were exercised constantly under real load. But 50/50 is the steady state, not the failure state. When a region actually degrades, traffic shifts to 100/0.

That transition is what you are building toward and it has to be tested deliberately. We ran chaos testing specifically for this situation. Cut one region entirely, verify the other absorbs full load cleanly, and confirm recovery when it comes back. If you haven't tested the 100/0 state, you haven't tested your disaster recovery (DR) system. Instead, you have tested your routing config. Multi-region is expensive to build and maintain. For a critical build-time dependency like this registry, it was the right call. But it should be a deliberate decision, not a default assumption.

Two failure modes in this design are worth being honest about, because neither shows up in a clean chaos test. The first is a failure that is not regional at all. The S3 incident hit both regions at the same time, because both depended on the same S3 behavior. Regional failover cannot fix that problem. Failover shifts traffic to the other region, which is failing the same way, so failover triggers there too and traffic shifts back. The automation keeps moving traffic between two broken regions and adds noise to an incident it cannot resolve. Route 53 behaves the same way at the DNS layer. When every weighted record is unhealthy, it returns all of them rather than none. When both regions degrade together, the cause is a shared dependency. The correct automated response is to hold traffic where it is and page a human.

The second failure mode is a health check that reports the wrong thing. Our /health endpoint confirmed that the application process was running, not that it could do its job. If the backend database in one region goes down, the application keeps answering /health with 200 OK while real requests fail. This is exactly the case for which regional failover exists, but Route 53 sees a healthy endpoint and keeps sending traffic to the broken region. The confirmation Lambda checks the same endpoint, so it would also report a failover into that region as successful. A health check has to exercise the functionality the service delivers, such as a lightweight database read, not just confirm the process is up. Deep checks carry their own risk. If the dependency they test is shared by both regions, they bring back the first failure mode.

DNS TTL is the single most common DR misconfiguration I have seen in otherwise well-designed systems and it is worth addressing directly. TTL controls how long a resolver caches a DNS record before requerying. If the setting is too high (e.g.,  three hundred seconds, six hundred seconds, or whatever the module default happened to be) and your failover logic can fire correctly, then your routing weights can update correctly and clients will keep hitting the degraded region for minutes because their resolvers haven't expired the old record. The failover executed correctly, but the traffic never moved because resolvers were still serving the cached record.

If the setting is too low, then you have built an overreactive system. A transient latency spike triggers a DNS change. The issue resolves thirty seconds later. Now you have regions flip-flopping and amplifying instability that would have cleared on their own. The right TTL is a deliberate number, chosen against your RTO, your health check interval, and your false positive tolerance. Most teams are running whatever default Infrastructure as code (IaC) module was set years ago. They don't know what that number is until they are debugging a failover that didn't go the way they expected.

Figure 2. DNS TTL and failover timing. A weight change that fires correctly can still leave traffic stranded in the degraded region until resolver caches expire. (Source: created by author.)

What separates DR systems that actually work from those existing only on paper is automation with confirmation, not just detecting failure, but acting on it and verifying the action succeeded. Most teams that have invested seriously in DR have detection, such as alerts that fire when error rates spike or health checks fail. Fewer have built the response layer, the automated action that runs when the signal fires. Fewer still have built the confirmation layer, the part checking whether or not the response actually worked.

This last piece matters more than people realize. Automated failover without confirmation is a system taking an action and then going quiet. Did the secondary region receive the traffic? Did DNS propagate before the TTL window? Are the downstream dependencies there responding correctly? A system capable of answering these questions by continuing to observe after acting is one you can trust. A system that only fires and then goes silent is an untested hypothesis.

The pattern looks like this in practice: A Prometheus alerting rule evaluates a composite signal, error rate above threshold AND p99 latency elevated AND sustained for a defined window. This observation is important. Single-metric alerts are noisy. A transient spike fires them constantly for things that resolve on their own in a minute or two. The composite condition with a duration requirement indicates you only trigger degradation that has actually persisted.

Most implementations stop at the alert. Here the alert is the entry point to an automated chain. How traffic moves depends on the topology. In an active-active setup, Route 53 does the switching. Each regional record carries a weight and a health check. When a region's health check fails, Route 53 stops returning that record, so traffic shifts to the healthy region with no custom code. In an active-passive setup, the alert drives the switch. Alertmanager routes it to a webhook, which invokes a Lambda function that flips the Route 53 failover record to the secondary region. In both cases, the alert also triggers a confirmation Lambda that polls the target region's health endpoint until it confirms the region is returning healthy responses. The human receives a notification only after the Lambda confirms the loop completed successfully. Detection, action, and confirmation form one connected loop. Observability drives the action and then verifies the outcome.

Figure 3. The detect–act–confirm loop. Prometheus fires, Route 53 shifts traffic, Lambda polls until the target region confirms healthy, then notifies the team. (Source: created by author.)

That confirmation loop, in practice, looks like this:

The loop does not close until the health check returns 200. If it never does, the function returns unconfirmed and that signal itself becomes an alert, not a silent failure.

This is a Terraform configuration for the Route 53 side. Both regions carry equal weight and Route 53 stops returning a region's record when its health check fails:

The by (region) clause is what makes this rule region-aware. It evaluates the composite signal independently per region, so when one region degrades while the other remains healthy, the alert fires with the specific region label that tells the automation exactly which region is degraded.

The for: 90s is doing real work there. Without it, this alert fires on blips. With it, the alert fires only when something has been consistently degraded for a minute and a half, which is a meaningfully different situation.

Finally, there is testing. The most effective practice I know for thorough testing is the game day,  a scheduled exercise where the team deliberately injects real failures into production systems and works through detection, response, and recovery in real time, with the people who would handle a real incident in the room. It is not a runbook walk-through in staging.

Game days find the human gaps as reliably as they find technical ones. Who actually has decision authority when you cannot reach the incident commander? Where is the runbook for this failure mode, exactly? Does everyone know? The first time most teams run one, the answer to these questions is uncomfortable. That is the point. Finding it during a game day costs an afternoon.

The validation that teams most consistently skip is testing that the confirmation layer correctly recognizes a successful failover and stops taking action. People test that the failover fires. They rarely test what happens if it fires and the system thinks it didn't work. That is a real path to cascading failures you created yourself.

The S3 incident wasn't something I had modeled. Nobody had a runbook for "S3 silently breaks concurrent signed URL requests under load following an internal deployment". The assumption that underpins a lot of how we build systems, that the infrastructure below us is basically reliable, is fine most of the time, which is exactly why it is so rarely questioned.

Three steps will turn your failover plan into a working system. First, pick one alert that pages a human today and wire it to an automated response with a confirmation step. Second, put your secondary region under real production traffic before you need it for failover. Third, on your next game day, test the confirmation layer, not just the trigger. Verify that the system recognizes a successful failover and stops acting. If you haven't validated all three, you have a plan, not a system.

Infrastructure will fail, and the next failure will probably be one you haven't seen before. Whether a person has to piece together a response manually or the system handles it was decided long before the incident started.

#10053. Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

Cybercriminals using agentic pen-testing tools is a proverbial genie out of the bottle at this point, so enterprises need to get a defense plan in place right away.

A month since it went closed-source, the Artex agentic penetration testing framework is spreading faster and causing more havoc than ever. Still, cyber defenders tell Dark Reading that defending against it is largely a matter of willingness, not capability.

To recap: In August, a Chinese open source (OSS) developer released a cybercrime-grade agentic red-teaming tool called "Artex." In the months that followed, attackers and cybersecurity researchers have gradually realized just how effective Artex is at probing for vulnerabilities and turning initial access into meaningful compromise at so-called machine speed.

"Artex is what the perpetual conflict era looks like," says Yuval Itzchakov, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of A Security. "When our research team ran it against our open source benchmark, it found eight vulnerabilities in about 45 minutes, including a critical privilege escalation to admin, and chained them into a full attack path through a WAF, CAPTCHA, and MFA. All it took was a download, an install script, and a model key."

Related:Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Nothing about it is so complicated, he says, "And that's the point. Take the guardrails off an AI hacking tool, and anyone can run agentic attacks at scale. In Artex, scope is just a suggestion to the model."

Though its author de-listed the original Artex on Oct. 8, new variants continue to cause trouble. The variant du jour, "AntiFox," was recently weaponized by attackers to exploit Internet-facing Web services and their associated Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. According to researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs, threat actors used their new agentic toy to breach, deploy Web shells, and execute operating system (OS) commands on compromised Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) servers, as well as enumerate services, expose production secrets, and manipulate Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets across AWS environments.

Notably, Arctic Wolf Labs offered relatively banal advice for organizations defending against this quite new threat: hunt for indicators of compromise (IoCs), rotate and revoke relevant credentials and sessions. In fact, researchers say, there's little more to defending against Artex or AntiFox than basic cybersecurity hygiene. However, it's also important to avoid making assumptions; as GitGuardian pointed out in a blog post on AntiFox, "Blocking scanner tools won't stop these agents, and a leaked key stays dangerous until someone revokes it."

The prospect of every Tom, Dick, and Harry having an agentic attack framework in their pocket might be intimidating, but cybersecurity defenders still possess some distinct advantages.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

First off, Itzchakov points out that "Artex stops at the front door. It has no lateral movement, no Active Directory testing, and no view inside. Defenders can see their whole environment and test it continuously with the same speed and autonomy, under guardrails no one can switch off. The organizations that come out ahead will treat this as permanent and build their security around it."

In a profile of a recent incident response (IR) effort against an Artex attack, Eye Research noted another serious weakness of agentic tools in general: They're loud. "The agents left their name in pod names and probes, hammered endpoints no human would touch, and tripped detections on systems with EDR installed," it explained. "Where we had visibility, we saw them immediately."

"If you want to be positive, there are a lot of small steps you can put together in order to protect networks and organizations," says Guillaume Valadon, lead cybersecurity researcher at GitGuardian. To catch Artex or AntiFox's loudness, for example, "blue teams must have in place a security information and event management (SIEM) platform and a really good detection system, to make sure that they will detect these tools in the noise."

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Besides active detection, organizations would be well advised to focus on secrets management. Artex and AntiFox have proven adept at finding secrets, in part because they use ordinary commands like "git" and "grep" to find what they're looking for, instead of shipping a more easily identifiable and blockable secret scanner.

"Defenders need to be looking for exposed and dormant keys, checking Git repos for exposed secrets, and heavily implementing a defense-in-depth posture," adds Justin Moore, Arctic Wolf's director of adversary operations. "What makes these frameworks so effective is not that they’re conducting novel attacks; they’re just doing what we already know, just faster than we have seen before. Good cyber hygiene is exactly what prevents these types of attacks from being so successful, whether they’re agentic or not.”

Despite all of the positive steps organizations can take, Valadon says, "If I'm being negative, I would say that it's too late."

"For years we have been telling people that they should not output secrets — that we're finding really important hardcoded secrets everywhere, publicly. On Docker, GitHub, and so on. Now, because we have these tools that can go fast from nothing to discovery to weaponization, that makes it more difficult for blue teams," he says.

"The agentic capacity for the attacker is already here, and they're going faster and faster and faster," he notes. "So if you didn't do the right stuff before, it will be difficult for you to catch up."

The cybersecurity industry has been waiting for AI-driven cyberattacks for years now. Product marketing campaigns have hinged on agentic attacks being right around the corner. Stories of lightly AI-influenced tactics, techniques, procedures (TTPs), and malware have kept food on cyber reporters' plates. Most of the discourse has been, at best, theoretical, at worst, misleading.

A meaningful, if incomplete, turning point seems to have occurred around midyear, if not among the most sophisticated attackers, then at least in the world of middling cybercriminals.

"When we all started using ChatGPT, at that time, we were just asking it simple questions. It was fun, but it was not possible to code," Valadon explains. "And then we had agents that were more capable at coding and syncing. This year you can do it all, from end to end. You just give [an agent] a rough idea, and it will do some planning, syncing, it will build the code for you, and deploy it for you. It's getting better and better at doing the whole cycle."

He also points to Anthropic and OpenAI's warnings about OSS AI earlier this fall: "Some people are saying that we are seeing these [attack] frameworks because of Chinese open-weight models. Because if you have a big GPU, you are able to run your own offensive models with Artex."

"It's getting more and more dangerous," he says. "It's all fitting into the HuggingFace, OpenAI, Anthropic narrative [warning against attackers] having access to real offensive tools."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
