#9994. Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Nigeria faced more than double the cyber threats of the previous year, with Angola and Kenya also in the top 5 most-attacked countries globally.

Organizations in Africa faced an average of 3,834 cyberattacks per week in October, a jump of 38% from a year earlier, making the continent the most-attacked region for the first time in more than a year.

Nigeria, Angola, and Kenya were among the top-five most targeted countries, with Nigeria topping the list with nearly 6,700 attacks targeting organizations in the country every week; that marks a 140% increase over October 2025, according to data published by Check Point Research earlier this month. The nations are among those rapidly pushing technological transformation of their infrastructure, expanding connectivity, investing in digital services, and putting sensitive data in network-connected applications and storage.

The fast transformation is exposing more opportunities for attackers, says Shayimamba Conco, chief technology officer and security evangelist in the Office of the CTO at Check Point Software.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"All this rapid digital expansion is now happening within the region, but then, at the same time, this [expansion] is outpacing improvements in security maturity," he says, adding that security improvements are uneven across the continent. "Yes, some areas — let's say for example, South Africa — it's adopting cybersecurity at a much quicker rate than the rest of the Africa region, but there will be those regions which are still lagging behind a bit."

The significant increase in average weekly attacks pushed African organizations past those in Latin America as the favored targets of cyberattackers. In the first quarter of 2026, Latin America averaged more than 3,000 attacks per week, surpassing the approximate 2,700 attacks targeting African organizations. In September, the two regions essentially tied in terms of attacks, with Africa once again becoming the most popular target in October.

Globally, organizations experienced an average of 2,550 weekly cyberattacks in October, down 9% from September but up a third from the previous year. While Africa encountered the most weekly attacks, both Latin America and Asia-Pacific regions saw a greater-than-average number — 3,483 and 3,436, respectively.

Globally, cyberattacks focused heavily on the education sector, with the average academic institution suffering more than 5,900 attacks per week, up a third from the same month in 2025. The education sector has topped the global list of popular targets every month, with organizations made attractive to attackers because of their large data sets and reliance on legacy systems, says Conco.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"There is a lack of budget when it comes to not just IT, but specifically cybersecurity," he says. "A junior IT engineer has to manage these vast environments, which are hard to lock down by nature, because you've got all these students who need access to all these applications and resources."

In Africa, however, cyberattackers most often targeted financial services, government agencies, and the energy sector, according to Check Point's data.

The countries are racing to improve their cybersecurity postures and address persistent threats. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) continues to work on the details of the nation's cybersecurity and cloud-sovereignty policies. Last month, Operation Serengeti 3.0 — a joint task force between Interpol and 20 African countries — led to the arrest of more than 1,500 suspects and the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds. In August, Operation Jackal IV targeted West African crime syndicates, leading to more than 200 arrests.

Check Point also flagged the use of AI in companies as a potential weak point, finding that about 2.9% of prompts to generative AI and large language models (LLMs) posed a high risk of leaking sensitive information. The risk is steadily increasing over time, from 2.3% in August to 2.5% in September.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Interpol has also observed that attackers are increasingly using AI in a way that has impacted African nations. In its African Cybercrime Assessment Report 2026, Interpol found that 55% of reported cybercrimes across Africa used AI to some degree.

"Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region," Neal Jetton, Director of Interpol’s Cybercrime unit, said in a statement in August. "AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. However, we see that when countries work together, cybercriminal infrastructure can be identified, disrupted and dismantled."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9993. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

The irony here is hard to miss. Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.

That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.

The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.

We’ve been writing about the ransomware-as-a-service supply chain here, including recent coverage of negotiation-related arrests and the FBI’s warnings to other groups.

https://cyber.murati.net/posts/shinyhunters-leader-arrested-fbi-warns-others

The irony Stalyn noted is real, but the line Dubrovsky drew in his book is genuinely important for incident response work. Communicating with the threat actor to de-escalate or buy time during containment is a different thing from facilitating a payment, and IR teams live on that distinction every day. What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Get your outside counsel involved in the ransomware response plan before you need it, not after the FBI shows up with questions about who said what on your behalf.

Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is visibility into what the group actually does to get in.

Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:

– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect, Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability. – Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early. – Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one transfer to be useful to the extortion side.

The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.

We covered the detection angle in more depth here: https://cyber.murati.net/posts/fbi-tells-shinyhunters-members-to-turn-themselves-in-after-recent-arrest

#9992. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9991. Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Bot-driven fraud and holiday social engineering attacks stretch across many weeks, straining security teams and small businesses alike.

Cyber experts have long drawn connections between the accelerated volumes of holiday shopping and threat actors looking for opportunities to take advantage, but as the festive season kicks off, it's important to remember that security posture during this time period is a marathon — not a sprint.

Verizon today published survey results for its holiday trends report, tracking the insights of 600 small business owners and decision-makers in the US. Of those surveyed, 11% said they have dealt with a cyberattack or data-security incident during the holidays, and a third expect to increase cybersecurity investments this holiday season compared with last year.

Meanwhile, managed security services firm VikingCloud this week published a report surveying security and IT leaders which made even steeper claims: a full 86% of respondents said their business has faced at least one successful cyberattack in the past 12 months, and a whopping 98% said at least one came during the 2025 holiday season. And the Retail & Hospitality Information Sharing and Analysis Center (RH-ISAC) last year said the holiday season continues to be the most active fraud environment from a defender standpoint.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

Some reasons behind the prominence of cyberattacks during this time period are straightforward: Many cybersecurity teams experience lighter staffing during holiday periods and weekends (leaving the door open for easier ransomware attacks). The chaos of the holiday season also means online services and retailers are inundated with activity, giving threat actors cover. And on the social engineering front, the holidays give plenty of pretext for threat actors conducting phishing campaigns (fake emails promising unbelievable Black Friday deals, charity scams, and so on).

Some teams may take this as a cue to prepare for a few select days or weeks of this last part of the year, such as Black Friday or the week leading up to Christmas. But new research around one narrow corner of the threat landscape suggests that may not be wise.

One of the less-discussed types of threat activity retailers face each season is an influx of malicious bots.

F5 today published a study dedicated to automated threat activity leading up to Black Friday. The report analyzed bot and automation traffic across three Black Friday shopping seasons (2023 to 2025) using data from F5 Distributed Cloud Bot Defense. It covers retailers in three retail sub-industries: fashion, e-commerce, and quick-service restaurants (QSR). The report's authors observed that overall automation rose across the three seasons, from 17.4% of transactions in 2023 to 18.5% in 2024, and then 28.6% in 2025.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

The types of activity differ across industries, but F5 observed bots being used for product scraping and inventory hoarding, credential stuffing and account takeover, fake account creation (to claim new user offers), and gift card cracking (inserting gift card numbers into balance checkers to test for valid accounts).

In terms of trends overall, cyberattackers are increasingly leaning toward Web stores over mobile APIs, and a broad rise in bot sophistication over time. But one of the most notable conclusions that F5 researchers made is that there's no single best date to defend. Attackers start their bot onslaught weeks before Black Friday, and continue it well into the weeks after.

As Sean Murphy, F5's field chief information security officer (CISO) for North America, tells Dark Reading, "The data shows that automated activity can be elevated well before the shopping weekend, and the busiest day for automation varied dramatically from year to year."

Bot traffic does not necessarily reflect all threat activity, but there may be a broader lesson here: that steeling your security hygiene for the holiday season is not a few single days or weekends to prepare for but a broader stretch of time that spans from early November to the end of the year. Murphy says security teams "should have monitoring and protections in place throughout the shopping season rather than scaling them up only for Thanksgiving week."

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

For those in ecommerce dealing with Web and mobile APIs, he urges ensuring protection isn't substantially weaker on one than the other.

"Web traffic had much higher automation rates among the retailers studied, but the report specifically cautions against interpreting that as evidence that APIs are inherently safer. Where API protection is weaker, attackers can shift toward that channel," he says. "And because the dataset contains both simple scripts and automation designed to imitate legitimate users, defenses need to account for a spectrum of bot sophistication rather than relying on a single detection technique."

Finally, he recommends organizations prioritize targeted employee security awareness and training, particularly for those teams handling customer accounts, payments, and other sensitive information. "Many attacks still begin with social engineering and credential theft, so employees need to know how to recognize suspicious requests and protect account access."

Chris Flood, senior vice president and CRO of Verizon Business, tells Dark Reading that small businesses can reduce their risk with four fairly simple steps: require multifactor authentication, train employees how to spot scams, keep guest Wi-Fi separate from payment systems, and keep software and devices updated.

#9990. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.

Why do I still own and use a computer for my business?

For every invention, product, or process that man creates, several other problems are created for him. There never seems to be an end. I am glad that humans are actually testing the vulns that are discovered by LLMs, but for how long will that be the case? How long until the LLMs themselves well be checking there own vuln discoveries, testing and deploying with no human involvement…….

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. Again.

So, what’s the patch record for Linux? search says patches published anywhere from 5~10 days after public notices are posted, not easy to match Microsoft’$ record…

Linux is starting to accept LLM vulnerability requests and they’re finding some flaws that have been around for decades. The total number is likely less, at least for the Linux kernel, but full distros use a large number of projects to create their OS and each of those pieces will have their own vulnerabilities.

See for example: https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/status/release/stable

That shows what’s currently being worked on for Debian. The first column notes the specific package the CVE refers to.

Should we call it a vulnerability if no attacker has any interest in it? I’m seeing a flood of vulns getting patched, but I’m not seeing a flood of vulns causing breaches…

If someone can make your mom stop, cry, and fork over a twenty to an animal shelter talking about puppies in a subway station, that is still a vulnerability of your mother, even if she is fortunate enough not to be approached on any one single given day of her daily commute.

I expect better analogies from you from here on in young man.

#9989. Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series examines the fallout from recent high-severity flaw disclosures, exploring how fears of AI-assisted exploits trigger widespread panic, operational disruptions, and growing warning fatigue.

The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month, it was PHP2Shell. This week, it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discuss last month's PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging AI would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency currently surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical an,,,m d operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Hi, and welcome to this month's installment of Reporters' Notebook, featuring reporters from Dark Reading, TechTarget Cybersecurity, and Cybersecurity Dive. I'm Fahmida Rashid, editor-in-chief of Dark Reading. This month, we are going to be talking about scary security vulnerabilities and the lessons we should take about how they're disclosed. So, joining me are Alyssa and Dave.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Why don't you introduce yourself quickly before we start the topic?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei: Sure. I'm Alissa Irei, senior reporter with TechTarget, covering cybersecurity news.

Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones: David Jones. I'm a reporter at Cybersecurity Dive

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: All right, let's get started. We had what researchers have been calling PHP2Shell, which were essentially two security vulnerabilities found in some versions of PHP. In some software, using PHP is pretty serious. We're talking memory corruption, the ability to run code on a Web server without logging in.NNNNNNNNNN

We know it was serious and pretty scary because, on the CVSS score, it was a 9.2 out of 10. That's pretty big news. And whenever you tell anyone that by exploiting vulnerabilities, an attacker will be able to run their code on the Web server without logging in, it gets people worried. I believe the patches were out. There was a whole coordinated disclosure.

TTC's Alissa Irei: This struck me as a pretty big deal. Our colleague James Walker wrote a couple of articles on the vulnerabilities themselves and also the disclosure process, which I believe got a little bit rocky in terms of accidental early disclosures on X, and then there was a lot of racing to patch and companies taking their websites down. But yeah, PHP is in use, in, I think, 70% of the world's websites.

Anything that enables remote code execution seems like a really big deal to me. So, I thought it was noteworthy. I know, Dave, your take seems to be a little bit "this meeting could have been an email." Maybe when all is said and done, it was somewhat overblown.

CD's David Jones: I thought it was absolute chaos. I'm still trying to understand exactly what happened last month because the initial rollout of the patch, the disclosure, as you mentioned, was more than a little rocky and the hype around the entire situation in terms of what was actually at risk. That was kind of a bit of a moving target.

We've had situations in the past where there's a lot of concern that you're going to have what is considered systemic risk on such a global scale that large institutions will not be able to manage that risk in a timely manner. Obviously, there are a couple of factors that kind of played into this.

One was the fact that AI was involved in the discovery. With the fact that malicious actors are able to exploit vulnerabilities faster than they ever have been before. There's a great deal of concern in terms of are you able to address these vulnerabilities in a fast-enough method to get those patched, tested, and verified before malicious actors have a chance to attack them? I think what we saw last month was just a lot of preemptive action where major institutions all over the world were basically preemptively taking their sites offline because they had no way of triaging the potential fallout in time to properly address whether or not they were fully protected.

It's still a bit of a mystery to me exactly what happened, whether there was an initial overreaction, whether there were elements of the exploit that we just didn't understand. There was a lot of bad code in a lot of the proofs of concept, and it just never quite amounted to the emergency that it was set up to be.

Maybe it was a good exercise. But we're still trying to get to the bottom of exactly what took place and how we can avoid some of the exaggerated threat that we saw.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: You brought up two really important things that I want to make sure we dig into. The first one was, there was a bit of a fear that because the adversaries have AI, we don't know how fast they're going to be able to launch an attack. And I think that was the reason for some of this panic … you know, take down the website so that we have time to figure it out.

With Log4j, what was it, three days before we started seeing proofs of concept? And I think there was this sense that we don't have those three days anymore. I think, Dave, you make a really good point that maybe this was a good exercise. Maybe we now know that at least for now, it will not be the same day. We're not going to see an attack the day we see the vulnerability.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Well, the tricky thing about that, though, is can we say that? Because AI can move so quickly, it can also move much more slowly than we anticipate. But is today the day? I do think that there's a big question mark around, you know, sophisticated machine-speed AI-enabled attacks that we're not seeing yet. But also, you don't want to be the organization that is the Wikipedia entry for the big one.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Yes. That's true. But I definitely do think that part of that entire response was driven with we don't know when those attacks were coming. But, Dave, you also noted a second point which I thought was really interesting. That even with AI, the exploit path was a lot more complicated to exploit. I think we've always said in our beat that just because there is a vulnerability, just because there is a way to exploit, does not mean it will automatically be exploited. Sometimes the process to do it is hard, and not all attackers are going to take that harder route. And I think this was an example.

CD's David Jones: I think, you know, in a way it's good that we're thinking about how we respond to these types of things. Maybe we're better prepared, but at the same time, I think we don't want to get into a situation where we're crying wolf ahead of time. And at the end of the day, what actually happened?

Was Black October deserved? I mean, was it really that bad a month? Because I've seen worse.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good point. It reminds me of, you know, national disaster weather warnings. At some point, if you go through enough of them and nothing much happens, people become inclined to ignore them. And at some point, that can be quite dangerous. So, I think it's a fair point.

Do you think that this sort of … I think we used the word hysteria in a previous conversation, communal hysteria, if you will. Do you think that this is specific to the AI age? It has this tendency to overreact. Has it grown in the age of AI and given us our fears about adversarial AI, or do you think that this is a pre-existing tendency that we as an industry have?

CD's David Jones: When you're a security team, particularly a security team with limited resources, you can't respond to every critical flaw or even medium- or high-severity flaw.

Whenever you want to, the resource is not there. You have to prioritize; you have to make decisions about the vulnerabilities that are going to affect the most critical technology.

Can I take the proper steps to either slow this process down or stop it before it gets out of control and I lose control over exactly how my operation continues? Because you have certain businesses where you may be operating in an OT environment where you can't afford to shut down for a certain amount of time. You may be running a hospital; you might be running a factory. You might be running fuel through a pipeline. You can't necessarily afford to be offline for a certain amount of time.

It's a difficult thing. I mean, there are probably a lot of organizations that were basically shut down for a certain amount of time, and they lost money, they lost time, they lost productivity. I don't think we can do that each and every time there's a critical situation.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: That's actually the one thing that occurred to me, when Web people were like, we need to take the site down while we figure things out. And I was like, just a couple of weeks prior, we had people taking down their Citrix boxes because there was a vulnerability and we didn't know what was going on. We don't know what's going on, so turn it off. And to Dave's point, we can't turn everything off. So, it's getting to be a priority, but to also understand when something is so bad that it is a turning-off incident. Because I'm worried that we're kind of moving into this state of turning it off every time, and that's just not practical.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: One thing I want to make sure we get a chance to talk about, and I love that Dave mentioned Log4j, because I think it's one of the biggest concerns. So, with Log4j, as a refresher for everyone, it was a vulnerability in a logging framework used by Java applications. And the challenge was that it's used in all sorts of different applications. And so, you could be like, nope, I looked, but I don't have Log4j, not realizing your suppliers were using it. And I think there was a bit of a worry that this might be the same, where I might not be using it, but I don't know who else is.

Which I think is a very legitimate concern. You need to know not just what you have, what your suppliers have, what your partners have. And I think that was the one aspect of PHP2Shell that kind of got a little obscure. That entire concept of thinking broader and bigger is something that really reminded me with this one that vulnerabilities are not just in your stuff; they're in other people's stuff too.

TTC's Alissa Irei: I think it's a great point. And I do worry about the smaller open source projects that have one or two maintainers, and it seems like everyone is drowning in vulnerabilities these days. And what does that mean for teams that are barely teams, and what does that mean for the software supply chain? I think it's a legitimate worry.

CD's David Jones: I'm not sure that a CISO or a frontline security operations team has the authority to take anything out of service without having a conversation higher up the food chain. I mean, you've got to be in a situation where … let's say there's an emergency, you've got to have people kind of above your pay grade where you have conversations where, yeah, we're not going to be producing food for the next few days, maybe. Or we've got to stop these surgeries if you're in a hospital system. The nuclear plant is not going to be, you know, cooling down for maybe a few hours. You've got to have this thought out in terms of, OK, can you explain to somebody who may not be a trained engineer, who may not be versed in these various systems, why you have to move forward and disrupt the entire business operation for a certain amount of time, because if you let it continue, and let's say somebody gets into your IT environment or your OT environment, and you may not be able to see them.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good reminder that ultimately a CISO's job in some of these cases is communicating risk, not deciding how to manage the risk. It becomes about being able to quickly and accurately communicate the operational risk to someone who is paid to make those decisions.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: We're increasingly seeing situations where the CISO is the one left holding the bag. So yeah, it's definitely a bigger calculation. To Alyssa's point, communicate it; make sure everyone understands what this means so that it's an informed decision.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Actually, this makes me think of two comments that have come up in recent conversations. DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: I think overall it's worth saying that yes, this is serious, yes, this is huge, here's a priority list. But you know what? Maybe it is the time to be a little bit contrarian.

Dave, what would you say is the one lesson you want our listeners, our readers, to be taking away?

CD's David Jones: Well, I guess the question I would have is: Are you prepared and properly set up to address such a situation the next time it happens, because it might happen over Thanksgiving.

Let's agree that AI has the ability to find critical flaws that might take a human team days, weeks, or months to find.

There are state actors and sophisticated criminal actors that can get access to an AI-assisted or automated attack. Find out how to best attack a vulnerability. That could happen within the space of days or hours.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Definitely. Alissa, what would you say yours would be?

TTC's Alissa Irei: Mine is much broader and much less useful.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: My thought was kind of similar to yours, that the fundamentals still matter. #9988. Implementing Table Partitioning in PostgreSQL

Database administrator with 14+ years of hands-on experience in database management and database design.

Database administrator with 14+ years of hands-on experience in database management and database design.

Database administrator with 14+ years of hands-on experience in database management and database design.

I have been running production PostgreSQL systems for over sixteen years, and if there is one lesson that never gets old, it is this: a table that behaves beautifully at ten million rows can turn into a nightmare at five hundred million. Indexes stop helping as much as they used to, vacuum runs longer, and every maintenance window gets scarier. When I see queries slowing down despite solid indexing, partitioning is usually the next tool I reach for. Let me walk you through how I actually implement it.

Partitioning takes one logical table and splits it into several physical sub-tables called partitions. From the application side, nothing changes. You still insert into and query one table name. Behind the scenes, PostgreSQL decides which partition each row belongs to and routes reads and writes there automatically.

I like to compare it to a filing cabinet with labeled drawers. If everything is dumped into one drawer, finding last year's invoices means digging through everything ever filed. Label the drawers by year, and you go straight to "2024" and search only there. That is the entire value proposition, in one image.

PostgreSQL, from version 10 onward, gives me three built-in partitioning strategies. I pick based on the shape of the data.

Range partitioning splits rows by a range of values, most often dates or numeric IDs. This is my default choice for time-series data, things like orders, logs, or events that accumulate by day or month.

List partitioning splits rows by a discrete set of values, like country codes or status flags. I reach for this when the data naturally falls into named buckets rather than a continuum.

Hash partitioning spreads rows evenly across a fixed number of partitions by hashing the partition key. I use this when there is no natural range or list to key off of, but I still want the data spread out for performance and manageability.

Here is how I would partition an orders table that is bringing in millions of rows a year. I will partition it by created_at, monthly.

Something worth keeping in mind here: the parent table never actually stores any rows. It is a purely logical container that PostgreSQL uses to route data to the right child partition.

One detail I always double check with new team members: the range bounds are inclusive at the bottom and exclusive at the top. A row dated exactly 2024-02-01 lands in orders_2024_02, not orders_2024_01.

I create indexes on the parent table, and as of PostgreSQL 11 they propagate down to every partition automatically. That saves me from having to remember to index each child individually.

I do not have to tell PostgreSQL which partition this belongs in. It reads the created_at value and routes it to orders_2024_01on its own.

This step is not optional in my process. I always verify pruning with EXPLAIN before I trust a partitioning setup in production.

If the setup is correct, the plan should only touch orders_2024_02. If I see the planner scanning every partition, something in my query or my partition key is off, and I go fix it before moving on.

If I am partitioning something like a customers table by region rather than by time, list partitioning is the right tool.

Each region code is explicitly assigned to a bucket, which makes this strategy easy to reason about and easy to explain to the rest of the team.

Sometimes there is genuinely no range or category to split on, and I just need the data spread evenly for performance and manageability. That is when I use hash partitioning. Here I am splitting an events table into four partitions by user_id.

Especially during development, or when I am not one hundred percent sure every possible value has a home, I set up a default partition to catch anything that does not match an existing rule.

This has saved me more than once from a failed insert at 2 a.m. because someone introduced a new status value nobody told me about.

I never want to be the person manually creating next month's partition by hand, and neither should you. In production, I write a function like this and schedule it.

I schedule this with pg_cron when it is available, or with an external scheduler like a cron job or Airflow when it is not. Either way, I make sure I always have a few months of partitions created ahead of time, so an inserting application never hits a missing partition.

This is where partitioning earns its keep for data lifecycle management. Instead of running a slow, lock-heavy DELETE that chews through WAL and leaves bloat behind, I just drop the partition.

If I need to keep the data around for archival purposes rather than destroying it, I detach it instead:

A few things trip people up every single time, so let me save you the pain.

Your primary key has to include the partition key. PostgreSQL cannot enforce uniqueness across partitions unless the partition key is part of the key.

Foreign keys referencing a partitioned table are not supported. Foreign keys going out from a partitioned table are fine, but nothing else can point at it with a foreign key constraint.

Partition pruning only works if the partition key shows up in your WHERE clause. Leave it out, and PostgreSQL has no choice but to scan every partition.

Do not go overboard with granularity. Hundreds of tiny partitions will hurt planning time more than they help. For time-series data, I have found monthly or quarterly partitions to be the sweet spot in most systems I have run.

When I want a quick sanity check on what partitions exist and how big they have gotten, I run this:

Partitioning is not free. It adds real operational complexity, and I skip it when any of the following apply:

PostgreSQL's declarative partitioning is mature and, honestly, not that hard to implement once you understand the shape of your data. Here is what I keep coming back to:

My advice after years of doing this: pick one table that is currently causing you pain, instrument it properly, implement partitioning, and measure the before and after. Once you see the difference for yourself, you will not need convincing on the next one.

#9987. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.
